#756. In Bulgaria, record low voter turnout triggers a November 1 presidential run-off in a poll colored by divisions over Ukraine war

Low voter turnout has triggered a run-off for the Bulgarian presidency. The vote was colored by strong divisions over Russia's war in Ukraine, and Sofia's relations with the Kremlin.

Record low turnout in Sunday's Bulgarian elections mean voters are expected to head to the polls on November 1 to cast ballots in a presidential run-off.

Polling stations opened at 7 a.m. and closed at 8 p.m. (0500-1800 GMT), with official results expected within 48 hours, but voter turnout was less than 40%, far short of the 50% required.

Voters were choosing between candidates with vastly different views of the war in Ukraine and relations with Moscow and the vote came as drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea off the Bulgarian coast brought home the significance of the conflict in Ukraine for the former Soviet satellite state.

Although the presidency is largely ceremonial, the head of state in Bulgaria can appoint interim governments during political crises, is commander-in-chief of the armed forces and is able to veto legislation.

Frontrunner in the elections is incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who took over the position this year after current Prime Minister Rumen Radev stepped down to take part in the parliamentary elections that led him to power.

Yotova, 62, who surveys show as having 41-47% of the vote, favors dialogue with Moscow as the way to bring peace to Ukraine and opposes military aid to Kyiv.

A win for Yotova would give a boost for Radev, who also advocates dialogue with Moscow. Victory would make Yotova Bulgaria’s first elected female president.

Her main challenger is Andrey Gyurov, a former caretaker prime minister, who is polling at 28-31%.

Gyurov, 50, who is backed by the pro-Western opposition, is an outspoken critic of Radev's foreign policy and strongly supports the Euro-Atlantic ties of Bulgaria, a European Union and NATO member state. As caretaker prime minister, Gyurov signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv.

The leader of the pro-Russian far-right Vazrazhdane party, Kostadin Kostadinov, is in third place on 10-13%.

Altogether 27 pairs of candidates for president and vice president are competing in the first round, with nearly half of them openly pro-Kremlin.

After casting her ballot in Sofia, Yotova called for peace, stability and unity, urging an end to divisions among Bulgarians. Her main challenger, Gyurov, voted in Blagoevgrad, calling for a Bulgaria that looks ahead and offers families greater economic security. Turnout was estimated at 15.1% by 3 p.m. local time (1300 GMT), according to polling agency Myara, Bulgarian media reported.

To win outright, a candidate must secure more than half the valid votes, with more than half of eligible voters taking part. Otherwise, the top two candidates advance to a runoff on November 1.

The war in Ukraine triggered by Russia's unprovoked invasion is one of the central themes in the election, particularly after four merchant ships were allegedly hit by drones off Bulgaria's coast this month in suspected spillover from the conflict. The attacks have prompted Bulgaria to seek assistance from its allies to strengthen maritime security.

Satellite internet antennas from the Starlink network — an important part of Ukraine's defense capabilities — were also set on fire near the capital, Sofia.

While Radev has said that the attacks seemed to be to the advantage of Russia and summoned the Russian ambassador, his government has declined to blame the incidents directly on Moscow.

The strikes have nonetheless raised concerns over Russia’s intentions to escalate the conflict.

Rising energy prices and inflation that have caused economic hardship to many in Bulgaria, the EU's poorest member state, are also a main issue addressed by candidates.

Many voters are also looking to stop government corruption, a persistent concern in the country, and hope for a stable government after multiple elections and coalition breakdowns in recent years.

#755. Carrick says it's 'crazy' but he's looking forward to Roma game

Michael Carrick signed a two-year contract in the summer

Michael Carrick accepts it might sound "crazy" but the beleaguered Manchester United boss says he is looking forward to the Champions League showdown with Roma at Old Trafford.

United go into Tuesday's game without a win in nine matches in all competitions.

It is their worst run since 1988-89. They have not gone 10 without a win in a single campaign since 1977-78 and there is a growing feeling Carrick will lose his job during the forthcoming international break.

Roma's only defeat so far this season was at home to Real Madrid in the Champions League last month, when they led 3-1 with seven minutes left.

United are 17th in the Premier League and after defeats by Atletico Madrid and Como have slumped to 21st in the Champions League table after three games, with only the top 24 making it through.

It is a bleak backdrop, but rather than fret over what lies ahead, Carrick is viewing it as a chance to change the narrative of the season.

"You might think I'm crazy with the results we've had and what's going on, but genuinely, I really can't wait for the game," said Carrick. "I'm really looking forward to it.

"Listen, I can't look into the future, you never know what's going to happen. That doesn't change the way I feel. Whatever happens is going to happen in whatever direction it goes in, but we want to make it a big night tomorrow."

Carrick watched over a lively open session of pre-match training at Carrington.

Striker Bryan Mbeumo and midfielder Carlos Baleba were particularly vocal, with Argentina defender Lisandro Martinez also fully engaged despite his red card at Chelsea, which triggered such a negative reaction.

While there have been calls for Martinez to be dropped for the Roma game, Carrick was more philosophical.

"Sometimes you do things; you make a decision, you make mistakes. Sometimes it goes well for you."

He also dismissed concerns both about Martinez's commitment, and that of his entire squad.

"Perceptions are a funny thing," he said.

"They can make things look all sorts of different ways. The dressing room is a good place.

"I've said it before, I don't question the commitment of the players, to the club and to me and to each other. We need to play better. We can make better decisions. But commitment's not a thing at all."

'You might think I'm crazy' - Carrick excited for Roma game despite struggles

England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo sat alongside Carrick at the media conference and also stressed the strength of the group.

Mainoo returned from a four-match absence with a muscular issue as a second-half substitute at Chelsea.

At 21, Mainoo is one of the youngest players in Carrick's squad. However, given he joined the club as a seven-year-old, he is also the longest serving and has a unique insight into the responsibilities that come with life in the Old Trafford spotlight.

"I've been at this club for a long time and know there's always going to be ups and downs," he said. "It's never going to be plain sailing and smooth to the top. You expect bumps.

"Of course it's been a tough season. We've not had the results we've wanted, but I feel like we're one win away from changing that."

United were last relegated in 1973-74. They have not been in the relegation zone after nine games or more since November 1986, when they collected a single point in Sir Alex Ferguson's first two games in charge following Ron Atkinson's dismissal.

Their lowest position after at least nine games of a season since then was 17th in 1989-90. They were 16th under Ruben Amorim after 37 games of the 2024-25 season.

Mainoo says the present position is unacceptable for a club of United's size.

"United's a huge club," he said. "I think a lot of people know the values this club holds and have been passed down through the people who've worked here and played here.

"I feel like I take some responsibility in spreading the word of what Manchester United is, coming up through the academy, and I plan to send that message for as long as I can."

#754. See Hoda Kotb & Ex Joel Schiffman Halloween Reunion With Daughters

Hoda Kotb and her ex-fiancé Joel Schiffman wore matching deviled eggs costumes while celebrating Halloween with their daughters Haley, 9, and Hope, 7.

Hoda Kotb and her ex-fiancé Joel Schiffman had an egg-cellent Halloween together.

The former couple reunited to spend the spooky holiday with their daughters Haley, 9, and Hope, 7, wearing matching deviled eggs costumes as they went trick-or-treating as a family.

In a video posted to Kotb's Instagram Oct. 31, the Today alum and Schiffman donned red devil horns and large cutouts of an egg, while their kids dressed as Poppy and Viva from the Trolls movies.

Posing in front of her home, Kotb wrote in the caption, "Happy halloween."

And this wasn't the first time the 62-year-old reunited with Schiffman, 68, to celebrate a special occasion with Haley and Hope. In September, the two were on hand to send their girls off to their first day of school.

"It’s here," Kotb captioned Instagram photos of the family drop-off. "4th and 2nd grade! Whaaaatttt?"

And though it's been four years since the former morning show host ended her engagement to Schiffman, her bond with the financier will always remain strong.

“I loved Joel then, and I love Joel now,” Kotb said on Today last year. “I just had to remind myself that it was a different kind of love.”

In fact, she believes their current dynamic is "the right relationship for us to have."

“We will co-parent in a beautiful way,” Kotb shared, “but I also think our ‘us’ is more of a, like, we’re dear friends now. And that’s beautiful, and it’s enjoyable and it feels right."

That's also because she and Schiffman are "honest" about their co-parenting relationship.

“Kids catch pretending. They know that Joel and I care so much for each other, and they also know that we love them dearly," Kotb added. “I really adore Joel, and they know it. I’m not pretending, I’m not faking it. So, once they see that, they go, ‘Ah, OK. This is good. This is good for us.’”

To see how other celebrities celebrated Halloween, keep reading...

The High School Musical alum and the baseball player were soarin', flyin' as Sally and Oogie Boogie from The Nightmare Before Christmas during Darren Dzienciol's Haunted Hotel presented by 1WIN and powered by Caliwater and LALO.

The Suite Life of Zack & Cody actor and the Victoria's Secret model also tapped into The Nightmare Before Christmas for Halloween inspiration, rocking Jack Skellington and Oogie Boogie costumes at their Sprouse House party with Raising Cane’s and Crazy Mountain.

Going goblin. The Hidden Figures actress enjoyed a BACARDÍ Rum cocktail during her Wondaween: Creature Camp celebration in Los Angeles.

The McCaffreys went from the field to the swamp this Halloween, transforming into Shrek characters. Culpo donned a Princess Fiona costume, while her husband rocked Shrek attire. But their kids and pup also joined in. Their daughter Colette dressed as a mini Lord Farquaad, while their baby boy Roman was the cutest Gingerbread Man. As for Donkey, their family dog had it covered.

You've got to hand it to the supermodel, who hosted her annual Halloween party on Oct. 31 in New York City.

The Watch What Happens Live host shared what was happening in a galaxy far, far away as he and his boyfriend Kevin Sobieski rocked Star Wars Jedi costumes, while his son Benjamin dressed as Darth Maul.

Feeling dirrty? The singer hosted her carnival-themed XTINAWEEN party with Raising Cane’s, MISTR, Astral Tequila and Crown Royal.

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star embodied some big Earth energy, dressing up as Mother Nature, while her kids joined in on the "chaos," wearing "volcano, thunderstorm, and tornado" costumes.

It's not her fault the singer dominated Halloween, with Rapp and her girlfriend Towa Bird creating a costume inspired by stylist Law Roach by dressing up as "law" and a "roach."

The former One Direction singer was feeling green this Halloween, appearing nearly unrecognizable as he transformed into Jim Carrey's character from 1994's The Mask.

Malik referenced the superhero comedy in his Instagram caption, writing, "Shombody shtop mehhh."

Dressed as Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman, the Bring It On star ran in her 54th birthday at a Halloween party with Crazy Mountain.

The rapper was in ha mood as Spongebob Squarepants' Patrick Starr at Unruly's annual Halloween bash presented by CH@Mobile and powered by Fanvue, LISTED and White Rabbit at Gravitas Members Club.

After dressing up as Belle, Hilton took her kids Phoenix and London out for some spooky fun at Night of The Jack, Los Angeles’ leading immersive Halloween experience.

#753. Who has made Troy's Premier League team of the week?

After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.

Here are this week's choices. Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page.

Bart Verbruggen (Brighton): He was unreal. Lots of saves which kept Brighton in it, even the last-ditch save where it hit him in the face.

Just an impenetrable wall. Brighton should really have lost by two or three goals, but Verbruggen was the reason they didn't.

Archie Gray (Tottenham): I'm going with a fully north London back four. Gray scored and defended really well. He was under a lot of pressure when Tottenham were in bad form and got a lot of stick, but now Spurs are starting to pick up I'm going to give him a bit of credit.

Ezri Konsa (Arsenal): He was a beast. Head it, kick it, throw your body in front of the ball. He defended and fought for the team, getting the job done.

Jan Paul van Hecke (Tottenham): Van Hecke got a goal and he's really growing into his role at Spurs. I still think he was a little bit overpriced, but all in all he's had a solid start, coming up with a few goals. Micky van de Ven next to him gives him confidence that he can go and be really aggressive, because Van der Ven will cover him with his pace.

Jurrien Timber (Arsenal): Timber got away with a shirt pull on Alexander Isak and I'm really surprised the ref and video assistant referee (VAR) didn't look at it. But again I thought he recovered and defended really well at full-back.

Romeo Lavia (Chelsea): I thought Lavia was excellent for Chelsea. People will turn to Manchester United having 10 men, but the 60 minutes before that Chelsea were all over the place. Lavia was the only constant breaking up play, keeping the ball moving. Plus he had an assist.

Declan Rice (Arsenal): A proper captain's performance, he gets the job done all over the pitch. He got a little assist for himself, too.

Tatsuhiro Sakamoto (Coventry): Sakamoto goes unnoticed by a lot of people, but I think he works really hard for the team and he is very humble in his approach. On Saturday he also delivered in a massive game for his team.

Johan Manzambi (Aston Villa): Another assist for him. He's a 21-year-old who is just flying. His confidence is through the roof and he is taking over this Villa team. Really good player, only going to get better. He was taken off thinking about the Champions League game against Barcelona, but up until that point Fulham couldn't really stop him.

Ollie McBurnie (Hull): Grafter, scrappy, endeavour, goals, assists... He had it all in his game.

He epitomises what Hull are: a player that's always overlooked, a team that's always overlooked, but they've got some spirit, some fight.

Taiwo Awoniyi (Coventry): Unbelievable solo goal. It's really good to see the big fella back playing and being in a situation where he can impose himself. If Coventry are to stay up, he's going to be why.

Frank Lampard (Coventry): He has been really good. Coventry have taken care of business against Sunderland, it's a massive six-pointer those games and his team came out front-footed, aggressive and also did a job on a very good Sunderland team.

Also a massive nod to Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta for getting the job done at Liverpool.

#752. Plaid Is the Ultimate Holiday Print—These Pieces Feel Chic Yet Festive

From tartan mini skirts to peplum hem tops, these plaid pieces make the perfect seasonal additions to your fall and winter wardrobe.

When it comes to seasonal fashion, certain styles just scream holiday dressing. Case in point, plaid.

Timeless with a preppy flair, plaid prints come around every fall and winter—and for a good reason. They feel festive yet chic. In other words, the pattern is on-season without making you feel like a walking decoration.

From tartan mini skirts to warm flannels and cozy loungewear, we found plaid pieces you'll rock all November and December long, from Thanksgiving dinners to holiday parties.

While plaid prints are already innately seasonal, certain color combinations feel extra festive. Think autumnal earthy browns and pops of orange or winter-ready reds like bright cranberry and deep burgundy.

Whether you're looking for the perfect plaid mini skirt to pair with your favorite knee-high boots or something cute to wear while you whip up a Thanksgiving feast, these plaid pieces add a hint of holiday cheer to your wardrobe.

With a woven twill fabric and buckle accent, this skort turns a schoolgirl staple into a sophisticated classic. It comes in both burgundy and navy blue.

We'd layer this button-up, body-hugging burgundy dress atop a warm ribbed turtleneck and pair it with your go-to knee-high boots and tights.

This plaid button-down, which comes in nine colors, can easily be dressed up or down. Made from an ultra-soft cotton blend, we recommend pairing it with some dark denim, suede booties, and gold accessories.

With its puff sleeves, peplum hem, and plaid smocked bodice, this red top with a romantic rose pattern is the definition of a holiday-ready look.

This mockneck frock features a subtle yet flattering ruched bodice and a trending drop-waist silhouette finished with a ruffle hem.

Fall festivities call for this burnt orange plaid top which has billowy, drop-shoulder sleeves and a relaxed fit.

It's not the holidays without some plaid pajamas. Soft jersey gives this button-up shirt and wide-leg pant set a relaxed, drapey feel made for getting comfortable.

Consider this your new wear-everywhere top, from office days to holiday shopping. The rich chocolate hue is totally on trend while a subtle peplum hem and flouncy sleeves give it an elevated feel.

Perfect for baking seasonal treats and opening presents on Christmas morning, this poplin shirt dress has a comfy oversized fit and combines a countryside-inspired print with a classic plaid pattern.

Elevate your nighttime routine with this soft knit robe featuring glamorous bell sleeves, a blue and green plaid print, and sweet lace trim.

Rihanna’s Savage X Fenty has matching holiday pajamas for the whole family, with cozy mommy-and-me onesies starting at just $25 for new rewards members.

#751. Who produced the kind of performance Moyes loves? - player ratings

Everton hold off Newcastle United to move in to seventh

A goalkeeping howler by Lukas Hornicek gifted Everton their first Premier League away win since February as 10-man Newcastle United slumped to a fourth defeat in six top-flight games.

Here's how I rated the Newcastle and Everton players, and you can see how you scored them below.

Grealish can still have Everton future - Moyes

Premier League: Everton beat disappointing Newcastle as Ramsey sees late red - reaction

Lukas Hornicek: Horrible mistake to allow Tyrique George's routine attempt to squirm under his body and present Thierno Barry with the goal. 4

Amar Dedic: A passing accuracy of 59.1% in the opening 70 minutes says it all. 4

Fabian Schar: Got forward and had three attempts but unable to help his side to a clean sheet. 5

Dan Burn: The Newcastle captain was booked for a foul on Barry right on the edge of the box. Fortunately for Burn, the set-piece came to nothing. 6

Lewis Hall: The kind of tidy performance we have come to expect from the England player. 7

Nico Gonzalez: Substituted as Newcastle slipped to an alarming fourth defeat in six Premier League games. 5

Joelinton: Produced one clever shot on the turn which looked to be heading for the net before James Tarkowski got in the way. Went close with another from distance. 6

Anthony Elanga: Came close to equalising when he kneed the ball on to the post before Everton just about got it clear. 5

Joe Willock: Replaced by Yoane Wissa. A long way short of his finest form. 5

Harvey Barnes: Lively start and the former Leicester winger went close to marking his 100th Premier League appearance for Newcastle with the 100th goal of his career. 6

William Osula: Was doubtful after twisting his ankle at Everton last week. Started but just seven touches in the first half. 5

Yoane Wissa (on 64, Joe Willock): Unable to find an equaliser. 4

Sean Steur (on 64, Nico Gonzalez): Could not influence the game. 4

Jacob Ramsey (on 75, Joelinton): Sent on to rescue the game. Got sent off. 3

Jacob Murphy (on 75, Anthony Elanga) Little impact. 3

Bazoumana Toure (on 87, Amar Dedi) Seven touches, three passes. 4

Subs not used: Nick Pope, Sven Botman, Aladji Bamba, Malick Thiaw.

Jordan Pickford: The former Sunderland keeper was predictable on the receiving end of relentless stick from the home fans but had the last laugh. 7

Jake O'Brien: Helped his side to a third straight Premier League win at St James' Park as the Toffees registered their fourth top-flight clean sheet of the season. 7

James Tarkowski: A commanding captain's performance as Everton won a Premier League away game for the first time since February. 7

Jarrad Branthwaite: Made a winning return to the side after missing the previous two matches because of concussion protocols. 7

Vitalii Mykolenko: Neat and tidy. Worked hard as the Toffees catapulted up the table from 14th to 7th. 7

Merlin Rohl: The German provided energy, got himself into some dangerous positions and went close with one attempt in the first half which cleared the bar. 7

Harrison Armstrong: Covered his face with his shirt after missing a great chance to put his side ahead on the stroke of half-time. 7

James Garner: A gritty performance, the type which David Moyes loves. Played his part in a fine away win. 8

Tyrique George: Heavily involved in the goal. It was his shot that led to the mistake that saw Everton take the lead. 7

Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall: Got stuck in and had an effort tipped over the bar. 7

Thierno Barry: Cannot stop scoring. Although this was the easiest goal he will ever score in his life after a goalkeeping howler. 7

Brennan Johnson (on 80, Thierno Barry): Helped his side get over the line. 5

Michael Keane (on 82, Jarrad Branthwaite): Helped Everton to clean sheet win. 5

Hayden Hackney (on 92, Tyrique George): Five touches, three passes. 4

Subs not used: Ainsley Maitland-Niles, Mark Travers, Tyler Dibling, Christian Norgaard, Charly Alcaraz, Braiden Graham.

After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users.

#750. Prague honors Roma resistance fighters against Hitler

More than 1,400 Roma fought against the German Nazi occupation in Czechoslovakia. A new exhibition in Prague showcases the stories of partisans and soldiers whose fates barely received any attention for decades.

For more than half a million Roma in Czechia and Slovakia, October 15, 2026, marks an important milestone.

That day, an exhibition on a largely forgotten chapter of Czech history opened at the Museum of the Romani National Revival in Prague. The exhibit explores the role of Czech and Slovak Romani resistance fighters during the Nazi German occupation and the dismantling of Czechoslovakia from 1938 to 1945.

Until now, Czech and Slovak Roma appeared in the history of World War II almost exclusively as victims of the Holocaust against Roma and Sinti. In the so-called Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia, Nazi Germany murdered approximately 90% of the Czech Roma during World War II.

However, what is less well known is that a large number of Czech and Slovak Roma fought against the German occupiers as partisans in resistance groups and as soldiers in the Czechoslovak Underground Army, or Defense of the Nation, ON.

The exhibition at the Museum of the Roma National Movement therefore marks a turning point in how the Roma are viewed during World War II. At least that is the hope of museum director Emil Scuka, a lawyer, former prosecutor and one of the best-known Czech Roma activists.

"We were not only victims; we were also heroes," Scuka said in his speech to several hundred attendees at the exhibition opening, most of whom were Roma from Czechia and Slovakia. "Many people, not even among the Roma themselves, are aware that we Roma fought against Nazism," he noted. In his view, "organizing and opening the exhibition was something my generation owed to these Roma heroes and today we are repaying that debt."

Scuka called on those present: "Bring your children and grandchildren here so they can see for themselves and realize that the Roma have heroes too!"

He also pointed out that this topic had been completely marginalized in Czech and Slovak historical writing for decades and that the Roma had therefore decided on their own to document the fates of their war heroes.

The exhibition presents the detailed life stories of 100 of the most significant Roma partisans and Roma soldiers from the Czech underground army and resistance groups who fought against the Nazis.

"We found over 1,400 Romani fighters in the archives. From among them, we selected the 100 most interesting stories for this exhibition," said exhibition curator Radoslav Scuka at the opening.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Among these figures is Anton Facuna, a sergeant in the American intelligence agency Office of Strategic Services (OSS), who was flown to Slovakia in October 1944 on a secret mission. Slovakia had been a puppet state of Hitler from 1939 to 1945.

Another is Josef Serinek, known by the nickname "Black Partisan from Vysocina," who managed to escape from the Nazi concentration camp for Roma in Lety and subsequently founded and commanded the large Capajev-Cerny partisan unit in the Bohemian-Moravian Highlands.

In 2022, Czech President Milos Zeman posthumously awarded him the Medal for Heroism. Toward the end of his life, Serinek shared his memories with historian Jan Tesar, who later wrote the three-volume book "Ceska cikanska rapsodie", which translates to Czech Gypsy Rhapsody.

Except for Tesar's book, the history of Roma resistance against Nazism has not been researched by Czech and Slovak historians to this day. "I am not aware of any scholarly historical work that deals with Roma resistance against Nazism," Prokop Tomek, a historian at the Military History Institute in Prague, told DW.

"The number of 1,400 Roma who took part in the fight against Nazism as members of the resistance or in the foreign army does not strike me as an exaggeration and corresponds to the proportion of the Roma population in Czechoslovakia," Tomek said, adding that the "exhibition on the Roma resistance against Nazism during the war is undoubtedly groundbreaking."

To this day, many Roma in Czechia and Slovakia do not publicly acknowledge their ethnic identity. This is partly due to experiences with the Holocaust during the Nazi era that have been passed down through generations. Czech historians and politicians continue to debate the extent to which the Czech authorities of the Protectorate were complicit in the extermination of the Czech Roma.

However, one thing is certain: the police registration of all Roma, which had been enshrined in law in Czechoslovakia since 1927, facilitated the extermination of the Roma by the German Nazis.

According to estimates by the Czech government, approximately 250,000 Roma live in the country today. In the 2021 census, however, only 21,000 people identified as Roma.

Of all ethnic groups in Czechia, which has a population of 10 million, the Roma are among the three largest ethnic minorities in terms of numbers. However, they are the most socially disadvantaged, have very little political representation, and are therefore scarcely present in Czech politics.

#749. From nightmare debut season to Everton hero - Barry's revival

Last season Thierno Barry scored eight goals in 41 appearances.

This season it's taken him just 12 games to match that tally.

On Monday night Barry scored against Newcastle for the second time in five days as his side earned a deserved win at St James' Park in the Premier League.

Only Erling Haaland (13) has scored more goals among Premier League players in all competitions this season than Barry (eight).

The 24-year-old is on his best run of form since joining the club from Villarreal last summer and, as Everton's only recognised senior striker following Beto's transfer to Fiorentina, is currently indispensable to the Toffees.

By scoring once again Barry highlighted why Everton paid Â£27m for a striker who grew up watching Wayne Rooney and Romelu Lukaku score for the Toffees.

The Frenchman had a rough start to life on Merseyside, having just one shot across his first 16 Everton games, and last month posted a video of himself breaking down during a private training session last season.

That moment was contrasted by his celebration on Monday night, which started with a knee slide and ended with dance moves.

"I was working a lot during the summer and now we can see the result," Barry told Sky Sports.

"The season is long but I'm happy to help the team with my goals.

"I want to enjoy more than last season and I enjoyed my celebration so I am happy."

It was a controversial strike though with Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle telling BBC Sport there was "a clear foul on Fabian Schar" in the build-up.

Who produced the kind of performance Moyes loves? - player ratings

Grealish can still have Everton future - Moyes

Jeers again as home woes continue - Jaissle has big problems at Newcastle

Everton hold off Newcastle United to move in to seventh

In the Premier League Barry leads the way for being involved in the highest proportion of his team's big chances.

Before Monday's match, Everton had recorded 24 big chances, and Barry had been involved in 15 of them (62.5%).

The striker has often been criticised for being wasteful in front of goal.

In Monday's match, for instance, he latched on to Jarrad Branthwaite's flick-on but, when through on goal, made a poor connection with the ball and scuffed his shot.

His goal - a tap-in from two yards - was very difficult not to convert, with the opportunity having had an incredibly high xG of 0.995.

"We know Barry misses chances, but we also know this season he keeps going and he scores goals," former Liverpool and England defender Jamie Carragher told Sky Sports.

His manager David Moyes added: "We're thrilled he's getting the goals because you need your centre-forward to score. He has missed a few but thankfully tonight he was on the spot to get the goal."

#748. Jeers again as home woes continue - Jaissle has big problems at Newcastle

Everton hold off Newcastle United to move in to seventh

If Matthias Jaissle was unsure what Newcastle fans thought of his team's latest error-strewn performance, he certainly knew at full-time after a second defeat by Everton inside a week.

Despite another miserable showing by Jaissle's side, the Toon Army had stuck by the team from start to finish before a chorus of boos echoed around St James' Park at the final whistle.

The frustration and anger from the stands came after a 1-0 defeat which included a goalkeeping howler by Lukas Hornicek, a red card for substitute Jacob Ramsey and another blunt attacking performance.

"Big frustration, big disappointment," said Jaissle after a fourth defeat in six Premier League games.

"After a performance like that I can understand the reaction from the fans. That's the reality and I am responsible for that.

"We need to work on the things we need to improve and after today that is a lot."

Newcastle's final game before the November international break is away to Fulham on Saturday, before facing Arsenal (home) and Brighton (away) when the Premier League resumes later in the month.

"It's not my first time as a manager in this situation," added Jaissle, whose side were eliminated from the Carabao Cup by Everton on Thursday.

"The only way is togetherness and showing unity."

Will the German - who became the Premier League's second youngest coach in the summer - find the solutions to get Newcastle's season back on track, with fans starting to run out of patience?

Who produced the kind of performance Moyes loves? - player ratings

From nightmare debut season to Everton hero - Barry's revival

No Premier League side has lost more home games in 2026 than Newcastle (7), while they have now lost 16 of their past 18 league games when conceding first.

The Magpies have failed to keep a clean sheet in each of their past 14 home league games - the longest run in their league history.

It all points to worrying times, with Jaissle just three months into a four-year contract.

"I fear a little for Newcastle," former Liverpool and England defender Jamie Carragher said on Sky Sports.

"They have a young manager and young players. You are always going to question the manager when the team is not winning.

"I think it is going to be a tough season. At home, especially, it feels flat and boring, and I never expected to say about Jaissle's Newcastle. You expected it to be front-footed and exciting, coming from the Red Bull model."

Newcastle are in the bottom half of the table, with 11 points from nine games.

It was always going to be a period of transition following Eddie Howe's exit, after five years in charge, and the arrival of 38-year-old Jaissle, after successful spells in Saudi Arabia and Austria.

In addition, Newcastle lost a number of key players in the summer including Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimaraes.

At the start of the year, Newcastle United's chief executive David Hopkinson said he could put them "in the debate about being the top club in the world" by 2030.

That now seems a long way off amid suggestions the ambitions of the club's Saudi Arabian owners, the Public Investment Fund, are running out of steam.

Jaissle was not helped on Monday by his goalkeeper, with Hornicek allowing a routine shot to squirm under his body for Thierno Barry to tap home the winner.

The Newcastle boss claimed Barry's winner should have been disallowed for a foul on Fabian Schar in the build-up, but he conceded his players had struggled to show the bravery required to get back in the game.

"It's almost like a negative spiral," he said. "I'm not happy with the referee decision.

"Unfortunately we couldn't deliver actually over the whole 90 minutes. It was not our game and our style of playing.

"That is something we are very frustrated and disappointed about. If you cannot deliver when it counts then you don't deserve to win.

"We were not brave enough in possession, too many long balls."

Jaissle admitted Newcastle are lacking belief in the midst of their miserable run.

"There are certain moments with not too much confidence, not only with the young lads but also with the more experienced ones," he said.

"It's a difficult period. We also know you can only overcome that as a unit. We worked hard and it looked good but unfortunately we couldn't deliver.

"We will analyse in detail and try and make things better against Fulham."

Matthias Jaissle post-match interview - Newcastle United v Everton

Newcastle have problems at both ends of the pitch.

While they have managed just 12 goals in nine league games, they continue to struggle to keep clean sheets.

They registered 17 attempts against Everton but only two of those were on target, and they have scored just once from their past 47 shots in all competitions.

Newcastle have faced the most shots of any Premier League team this season, including 15 or more in seven of the nine top-flight matches they have played.

While only Sunderland (6) and Hull City (5) have committed more errors leading to goals in the Premier League this season.

Meanwhile, this was Everton's first top-flight away win since February - when they won at St James' Park.

"I've been a fan so I understand the frustrations when they're not getting what they're expecting," said captain Dan Burn after the game.

"You can sense that nervousness in the ground.

"When you're not winning games there's always a lack of confidence. The fans weren't happy. That doesn't make it easy to build confidence when you're in that atmosphere.

"Between the boxes we do OK, but we're not ruthless enough going forward or defending our own box."

Jaissle added: "When the goals are not coming easily then you lack confidence. You have to stick together."

#747. Kraft Drops Cinnamon Roll Mac & Cheese—and the Reactions Aren't Grate

Kraft dropped a surprising new lineup of limited-edition flavors—including mac and cheese that tastes like a cinnamon roll—which has garnered a big reaction from foodie fans.

The instant mac and cheese company was certainly thinking outside the box when they came up with one of their new limited-edition meals: Cinnamon Roll Kraft Mac & Cheese.

"Yep, you read that right," the brand teased on Instagram Nov. 2 alongside images of their festive new flavors' packaging. "Chili Crisp and Cinnamon Roll Kraft Mac & Cheese are available now for a limited time."

And while fans were cheesing over the announcement of another spicy flavor to follow their cult-classic jalapeño release in 2024, there were quite a few questions about the other product’s unexpectedly sweet noodle profile.

As one user put it, "Okay but why are you like this?" while another referred to the end of daylight saving's time when joking, "It was a time change, not April fools day!"

In fact, the experimental seasoning had the internet likening Kraft to mad scientists. To express their bewilderment, one X account replied to the news with a Jurassic Park meme in which Jeff Goldblum muses, "Your scientists were so preoccupied with whether they could, they didn't stop to think if they should.”

“Yall are out of your minds,” one person commented, as another quipped, "I’m calling the police.”

Still, some die-hard mac and cheese lovers were excited to roll with the dair-ing new addition.

"Everyone thought the apple pie one a year or two ago was weird, but it honestly was pretty good," one snack enthusiast replied on Instagram. "I’ll give cinnamon roll a shot!”

Another user admitted, "I... I need to try this. For science."

And as adventurous eaters know, noodle dishes that cater to the sweet tooth have been around for some time.

"Kraft cinnamon roll mac and cheese is going to be good and I'm not apologizing for that," an X post riffed. "Sweet plus cheese is not some new crime. Cheesecake exists, noodle kugel exists, half of you put syrup on a sausage biscuit."

#745. ‘My Whole Life Has Been the Audition’: Jake Shears Talks ‘Rocky Horror,’ Tim Curry & His ‘One Request’ About Callbacks

The Scissor Sisters rocker currently stars as Dr. Frank-N-Furter on Broadway.

Although fans have been cosplaying as Dr. Frank-N-Furter for half a century thanks to The Rocky Horror Picture Show’s infamous midnight screenings, stepping into the mad scientist’s spangled heels remains a tall order for one reason: Tim Curry. Both on stage and on screen (The Rocky Horror Show debuted on London’s West End in 1973; the Jim Sharman-directed film released in 1975), Curry used his mellifluous voice, wildcat mannerisms and wicked wit to craft one of the most unforgettable characters of all time.

Curry’s Frank was easy to swallow but tough to follow — many who have laced up the corset since then have glimmered, but always in Curry’s shadow. When Jake Shears became the third actor to portray Frank-N-Furter in the current Broadway revival of The Rocky Horror Show at Studio 54, his debut took on a sad, sweet resonance, happening just weeks after Curry’s death at age 80. (Curry passed away on Aug. 25; Shears debuted on Sept. 11, taking over from Paul Soileau, who followed Luke Evans’ Tony-nominated turn.)

“If you’d told me when I was 15 that I’d be in the theater rehearsing for it on the day [Curry’s death] happened — to be able to share that moment with everyone else and be in the theater even now — it feels like a living memorial in a way,” Shears tells Billboard.

It may be a living memorial, but don’t get it twisted: this version of the sci-fi/horror/musical is no hushed, reverent recreation. Directed by Tony winner Sam Pinkleton (Oh, Mary!, Ta-Da!), this production leans into DIY set design, hodgepodge casting and playful camp to reanimate a show that remains as transgressive and titillating as ever. Eight times a week at Studio 54, the Scissor Sisters rocker-turned-actor brings his sly, bratty take on the Sweet Transvestite from Transsexual Transylvania to life.

As he packed his go-to bag ahead of a Tuesday night performance, Shears spoke to Billboard about his lifelong obsession with Rocky Horror, what he thinks about the audience callbacks and how Curry’s death affected his take on the role.

What’s your backstory with Rocky Horror? Is this something that’s been with you throughout your whole life?

I’m a true Rocky Horror nerd. I don’t think there would be Scissor Sisters without Rocky Horror. I don’t know if I would be a performer without Rocky Horror. I discovered it for myself when I was 12, just about to turn 13. For its 15th anniversary in 1990, they were putting it out on VHS. In celebration of that — I was an avid MTV and VH1 watcher at that age — I started seeing imagery from it and became really, really curious.

Right — it was a late arrival to VHS and a big thing when it finally came out.

My mom wouldn’t let me watch it, and it became a real point of contention between us. So my parents went out of town, and my older sister got me the soundtrack of the original Roxy cast from Los Angeles. That was the first time I heard the songs. Then when my parents were out of town, my sister got me the VHS tape, so I got to see the film for the first time and it just blew my mind. I immediately started figuring out ways to go to the Saturday night screenings, and I became obsessed with it. I’ve always been obsessed with it. It’s always been a part of my fantasies. I think it’s the greatest movie ever made. I think it’s the greatest musical ever made. There’s something about the script, the story — it is so magical.

This may be a digression, but Rocky Horror feels to me like a theme park ride. There’s so much going on in it, and there’s this underlying story happening underneath that you only get glimmers of. There’s something about the show that really spurs your imagination on. Your brain fills in so many blanks in Rocky Horror. I think that’s one of the reasons it’s touched so many people. I love that it’s kind of amoral.

The combination of all those things really affected me as a 13-year-old. It was also my first sort of dawning — it was my first “it gets better.” In my book [Boys Keep Swinging] I wrote about it like a message in a bottle, saying, “Hey, we’re out here.” It was like a message from my future. To me, it’s a sacred text. It’s my Rosetta Stone. Getting to do it [on Broadway] is a really deep, deep thing for me. I still kind of can’t believe it, and I don’t know if I’ll ever do anything that will make me as happy as what I’m doing now.

That’s beautiful: 12, 13 is such a formative age. To grow up with that, have it inform your outlook and then step into the heels. How do you top that?

There isn’t a way to top it. The other fun thing is that I love theater so much, and I love the repetition of it — the absolute grind of it. When you’re doing a five-show weekend, the whole thing turns into one big funhouse mirror. It gets weird. It really does put you in another kind of reality, and getting to do that in this world, with this show, feels like getting to step off the ride at Pirates of the Caribbean and go snoop around the animatronics.

That’s a great way of describing it. When they reached out to you for the role, how did that work? Did you have to do an audition?

I think my whole life has been the audition. But no — I got a call from a producer friend I’ve worked with, who said, “The Rocky Horror folks are looking for you. Do you want me to give them your number?” And I said, “Yes, yes, please.”

I was super secretive and kept it really close because it was such an exciting prospect. I had to protect myself — I could potentially be absolutely devastated if it didn’t go the right way. I’d been sitting around in London so jealous that it was happening in New York. Everyone got an earful around my kitchen table about how badly I wanted it. I was having a lot of FOMO that it even existed. A lot of my close friends were weirded out by the whole thing, because it felt like something I’d put out into the universe and then the universe hit me up.

As you were preparing for the role — between the announcement and your official stage debut — Tim Curry died. Did that change your preparation? Did it change your relationship to the role?

It did a little bit, yeah. It made me not be in denial that Tim Curry has always been in my DNA. It’s always been in my bones. So it’s made me not be super scared of that. I’ve definitely got my own spin on it. But I’m also not afraid to deliver his versions of the songs. There’s no escaping that.

They’re so iconic. But your performance does have its own flavor.

[Laughs.] How else do you do eight shows a week?

No, no — I just mean I’ve had a lot of fun thinking about the fact that we’re in Studio 54. I’m paying my respects to the ghosts at 54. We’ve got the moon in there. The spoon’s not there, but that’s been a part of the development of my Frank — Frank is really partying during this night. It’s been really fun to dig in and shape that. Please don’t write that I’m a cocaine addict.

Let the record state that you are simply making a reference to Studio 54’s snowy past, not talking about your own habits. You’re doing so many performances in such a short time. There’s that element of exhaustion, but you are going full force at the same time.

Yes. That’s the fun thing — you get to “Wild and Untamed Thing” at the end, and on a Sunday night I’m exhausted. But I love going into that show with barely anything, where you’re scraping the barrel a little bit and you just have to start and ask, “Where is this going to come from?” That’s always real, and it’s fun to dig around and figure out where that comes from. It’s feral. I love that I get to be absolutely feral on stage and a little bit out of control. There are moments in the show where I feel a little bit out of control.

I can’t help contrasting this with when you played Charlie in Kinky Boots on Broadway, which is such a buttoned-up role.

Oh my God, it’s the exact opposite. But it was amazing I had the opportunity to do that. Before that I did Moisés Kaufman’s Bent in L.A., and I didn’t know how to walk across a stage — I really didn’t know what I was doing. It’s been so delightful in my life to learn this skill. I love being in musicals, I love doing theater. And without doing Charlie in Kinky Boots — which is very buttoned-up, very opposite of my own personality — and without doing the Emcee [in Cabaret on West End], I don’t know if I was ready to do Frank until now.

Without Cabaret, this might have been biting off too much. I saw Tom Hewitt do this; I saw the 2000 version [of The Rocky Horror Show] on Broadway. I moved to New York in ’99. I’ve always thought about that production, always thought about Frank-N-Furter in it throughout my life and thought, “Oh, I wonder if I could do that.” My answer was always, “I don’t think I’ve got the skill. I don’t think I’m capable.” But in the last couple of years I’ve finally come to it. I think 48 is a great year for Frank, too. I don’t know if you can really have a 32-year-old Frank-N-Furter.

Did you talk to Luke Evans or Paul Soileau before taking on the role?

Oh yeah. Luke let me hang out in the dressing room and talk through stuff, and Paul too — both of them were extremely generous. We had a dialogue about the whole thing and still do.

After Tim died you three took the stage together and sang “I’m Going Home,” which was so beautiful. How did that come about?

It was the day Tim died — it was that night. Luke had just said his goodbye; they’d recorded the soundtrack, and Luke had said goodbye to Rocky Horror with tears and everything. Then, next thing you know — Luke hadn’t left town yet, so he was able to step back in. Paul was playing Frank that night, and I was sitting there rehearsing. It was the perfect little moment for us to be able to do that. It was very, very sweet. I’ll never forget it.

How did you feel when you finally debuted in the role?

What was really funny was that when I went into the show — my first Friday night — I had zero nerves. I had a great time, so much fun and I thought, “That’s so crazy. Where is this coming from?” I was very chill. And then the matinee the next day, I was absolutely scared out of my mind. I don’t know why. The nerves came. It’s funny how that happens — there’s no rhyme or reason.

I can see it, because Frank-N-Furter is such a creature of the night, literally. It makes sense for an evening, but it’s a very strange show for the afternoon.

Yes. Star Quezon, who’s amazing in the show with me and plays one of the Phantoms, turned to me after a weekend matinee and said, “It feels like it’s three in the morning.” It was so true. The matinees definitely have a very surreal quality to them.

You mentioned the nerves hitting the second time you performed. Do you have preshow rituals, anything you do to get yourself in the head space?

Once my wig is on and I get the boots on — the heels on — I pace around and make really f–king bizarre faces in the mirror and talk to myself for a while.

I make sure the dressing room door is shut.

I know the Narrator handles a lot of the audience callbacks, but has it been an additional curveball that the audience is periodically talking at you, shouting things?

It’s my favorite thing about this show. I love it so much. It’s only a curveball if the audience doesn’t know what they’re doing — that’s when it’s a curveball. I love the callbacks, and I really encourage them. I just ask that it’s not for amateurs. If you’re going to play with me on stage, do it confidently, clearly and know what you’re doing. That’s my one request. I’m down to clown and when it’s good, it’s really good. So I encourage it, but I also encourage those who want to participate at a higher level to really know what they’re doing.

Rocky Horror is a ritual in a lot of ways, and if you don’t know the beats, it’s not going to hit. And you’re at a Broadway show.

Exactly. And technically, callbacks don’t really work when the songs are on because nobody can hear them. So it’s best to stick with the moments when dialogue is going. But I personally love it. My favorite thing is getting surprised when somebody does something really funny that I didn’t expect. I’ve broken a few times on stage.

What has it been like working with Sam Pinkleton on this? I interviewed Sam before Rocky Horror opened, and he’s such a brilliant creative — a perfect mind for something like this.

Sam is so sweet and smart and fun to hang out with and work with. I think he’s amazing, and I think so many other people would follow him anywhere. He’s got a perspective and a humor that is so singular. I adore him and love being around him. It’s a blast. Like I said, me and so many others would do whatever.

He’s doing Annie next — you could literally switch from one Tim Curry role to another.

Oh God. I’m very excited about that show. I’m so curious to see what he’ll do.

Do you have a favorite song to sing in this performance? One that means the most to you?

“I’m Going Home” makes me emotional singing it pretty much every time. For me, it’s this crazy intersection of singing this queer hymn — it feels very spiritual to me — and, just after Tim’s passing, feeling so lucky to get to do what I’m doing. Being there, knowing how important it is for so many people in the theater and looking down at the people who got front-row tickets, at their faces — it’s a really special moment. I love singing it.

It feels that way. I love every song in the show, and I’ll never get sick of the music, but I especially love that one. The show is so chaotic in so many ways, so it’s really nice to get to sit down and sing something very still. There aren’t too many moments like that in the show, so it reverberates.

Do you think your feelings toward Rocky Horror have changed now that you’ve stepped into the world of it, as opposed to experiencing it as a fan?

Only in the way that it’s made my appreciation for it go even deeper than it ever would have. My imagination with the show has gotten deeper — my fantasies about the show, these characters, what they’re doing, where they’ve been, what the hell is going on. There’s a whole story going on that you just step into and witness, and you have to fill in those blanks. That’s the magic of it.

#744. The Neighbourhood Reacts as ‘Sweater Weather’ Makes Spotify History: ‘It Feels Bigger Than the Band at This Point’

The 2012 single is the streamer's most playlisted song of all time.

With sweater weather season in full swing, The Neighbourhood‘s signature song of the same name is reaching new heights on Spotify in 2026 — and nearly 15 years after its release, the band still can’t believe how fans are still warming up to it.

“Sweater Weather” officially surpassed five billion streams on the platform on Monday (Nov. 2), Spotify confirmed to Billboard, making it just the third song to ever hit the milestone. The mellow track is also the most playlisted song of all time on the streaming service, appearing on more than 103 million user-created playlists.

That’s a long way to come for a song that started as an idea between bandmates Jesse Rutherford, Zach Abels and Jeremiah Freedman when they were teenagers. “It’s still hard to wrap my head around,” Abels tells Billboard of its ongoing success. “We wrote it in my mom’s living room when I was in high school, and now it’s up there as one of the most streamed songs.”

“The song really took on a life of its own through the internet and fans — it feels bigger than the band at this point,” the guitarist continues. “We’re just grateful … People seem to put their own meaning on it, which is probably why it keeps connecting.”

Released ahead of The Neighbourhood’s debut album, I Love You, “Sweater Weather” peaked at No. 14 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 2013 and reached No. 1 on the Billboard Alternative Airplay chart. It has experienced a resurgence just about every autumn since, first hitting one billion Spotify streams in 2021. According to the platform, the song’s annual streams have increased by more than seven times over between 2019 and 2024 alone.

“I think it fits the season,” Abels says of why “Sweater Weather” has become an autumn staple. “There’s an intimate mood to it that people seem to want when it gets colder. Every fall the streams jump, and it ends up on a ton of playlists. We didn’t plan for it to become a seasonal thing, but it’s been consistent for years now.”

He adds, “The hook is very visual and physical, but the overall feeling is pretty universal — that mix of wanting comfort and closeness while everything else feels a little dark.”

It’s not only on Spotify that “Sweater Weather” is carving out an enduring legacy. Just a couple of months ago, the track’s visual surpassed a billion views on YouTube.

With the track still going strong, The Neighbourhood has released four more albums since its I Love You days. Most recently, the band unleashed Ultrasound in November 2025, peaking at No. 20 on the Top Alternative Albums tally; it soundtracked a sold-out world tour across Australia, New Zealand, Asia, Europe and North America

Add your stream to more than five billion others by checking out “Sweater Weather” below.

#743. Tech CEO Adam Robinson Among 9 People Killed in Florida Plane Crash

The victims of a Florida plane crash that killed nine people on Nov. 1 included tech CEO Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharpe and their kids Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2.

More details about the nine victims who died in a Florida plane crash on Nov. 1 have emerged.

Tech CEO Adam Robinson and his wife Helen Sharp—along with their kids Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2—were among the passengers on a Learjet 60 that nose-dived into a Palm Beach County neighborhood, according to a joint statement released by the victims' families Nov. 2.

The Robinsons' nanny Anita Maria Cetina as well as friends Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr were also aboard the aircraft.

"Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever," their family said. "Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives. Their loss will be felt deeply by all those who loved them and who they loved in return."

Meanwhile, Cetina "cared for Emma and Charlie with tenderness and devotion, and she was truly part of the family."

"She showed us a legacy of unconditional love and devotion," the statement continued, adding that Reed and Fehr "were full of joy and adventure."

"They loved their people fiercely, fully and without hesitation," their families shared. "From the moment they met, they were all in on each other and the life they were building. They are deeply loved, and we will miss them endlessly."

The fatal crash occurred around 12:51 p.m. local time after the flight crew aboard the private jet—which took off from Austin Bergstrom International Airport in Texas bound for The Bahamas—reported ice amid "moderate turbulence," National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said in a Nov. 2 press conference.

Chapman said ice was "certainly a factor" that played into the crash, though an investigation is still ongoing.

"The factual details of how this transpired is exactly what we're trying to determine," he told reporters. "The weather conditions are a major focus of the investigation."

While officials have not released the identities of the flight crew, a manifest obtained by CBS News identified the pilot as 55-year-old Jeffrey Gregory. His co-pilot was identified as Nathalia Filgueiras by her family, who said the 20-year-old earned her pilot license while still in high school.

"Flying was her biggest passion,” her older sister Giulia Filgueiras told NBC News Nov. 2. "That was her dream, to become a pilot, since she was very young."

The French government says more than 1,000 people were arrested following nationwide protests on Saturday. Police and elite security forces were out in force across the country as clashes broke out.

This blog is now closed. Thank you for reading.

You can read all our updates on the protests and unrest in France and other parts of Europe on October 24 and 25, 2026, below.

Marine Le Pen launched her fourth bid to become president of France on Sunday with a plea to "French patriots" to back her and her far-right National Rally (RN) in spring elections.

The grande dame of the far-right, Le Pen delivered an impassioned invocation of French spirit in Orleans, calling for "a renaissance" of the country's virtues and stressing its rich creative and intellectual history.

She blasted "Little Marquis Macron" and the state of France under his stewardship — both domestically and internationally — offering a fiery outline of the need to restore order, but also civility in the country, alongside promises of maintaining French (nuclear) defense and judicial sovereignty.

Le Pen said "we'll protect our public spaces so that they can remain places full of life and mutual respect" and cited civility as the surest way to keep violence out of society.

She praised regionalism over globalism or supranationalism in the form of the European Union (EU), and spoke of the need to defend freedom and the "French way of life," making clear that, "In France, you live like the French."

Le Pen recalled General Charles de Gaulle several times throughout her speech, emphasizing the historic importance of the moment when it comes to securing the promise of the future.

After ending her remarks with a full-throated "Vive la France!," a relieved-looking Le Pen was joined on stage by heir apparent Jordan Bardella and party members for a rousing rendition of the national anthem under the campaign slogan, "Pour la France La Renaissance."

Amid the latest demonstrations, what's driving the unrest, and could a broader youth-led protest movement be taking shape?

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

French unions and protest groups have called for fresh demonstrations on October 31 and a nationwide strike on November 5 to maintain pressure on the government.

The left-wing Solidaires union federation said anger over wages, living costs and public services was bringing together students, workers, firefighters and other groups.

"We see an aggregation of anger," Solidaires co-leader Murielle Guilbert told broadcaster BFM TV.

The SUD Education teaching union said it would join the October 31 demonstrations. The larger CGT union is set to decide during the week.

The Yellow Vests movement also called for rallies, including sit-ins outside town halls and the National Assembly.

The government has opened talks with unions and student representatives, but protest leaders say its proposals are inadequate.

French authorities detained 1,314 people during nationwide protests on Saturday, according to a provisional Interior Ministry tally.

The ministry said 53 police officers and other security personnel were injured, firefighters responded to 75 fires and 24 businesses were looted. It did not provide a figure for injured protesters.

Clashes broke out in cities including Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux, Toulouse and Tours, with police using tear gas. The ministry blamed groups including radical far-left activists for confrontations along or near protest routes.

Authorities counted 410,000 participants at 289 demonstrations and gatherings, down from 550,000 a week earlier. Other estimates put Saturday's turnout as high as 800,000.

The reported arrests and violence were substantially lower than on October 17, when authorities recorded 2,628 detentions and 1,144 injured security personnel.

The ministry said several investigations had been opened and described the subsequent night as calm.

With Saturday's protest over, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez reported nearly 1,000 arrests.

The number is expected to rise as security officials tally up the day's events, Nunez added.

"Multiple lootings have been averted," he said.

While some clashes between protesters and police were reported in many French cities, the scope of the unrest was much smaller compared to the protests last Saturday, which saw buildings defaced and burned, and some 1,500 shops looted across the country.

Nunez previously put the number of people arrested last weekend at 2,700.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Some 410,000 people marched across France on Saturday, according to the country's interior ministry, as the country braced for a possible repeat of violence seen last weekend.

In Paris alone, at least 110,000 ‌people turned out to denounce rising ⁠living ⁠costs and growing inequality.

Police were out in force in major French cities. While rallies in Paris and Marseille were mostly peaceful, clashes between protesters and police were reported in towards the evening.

Riot police in Paris fired tear gas and water cannons at some 500 hooded youths before they eventually dispersed. In Marseille, youths blocked roads by setting trash cans on fire. They threw rocks and bottles at security forces.

Clashes were also reported in the cities of Lyon, Bordeaux, Grenoble, Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Rennes, Nantes and Toulouse.

France is known for its protest culture, where demonstration is considered a bedrock value.

Altercations between the police and demonstrators are by and large part of the French protest ritual.

What we are seeing could even be considered a relatively calm end-of-demonstration situation, Lisa Louis, who is in Paris, said.

Meanwhile, security guards were deployed in Milan on Saturday amid demonstrations against the rising cost of living.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ordered 500 soldiers to be dispatched to the city, in addition to about 5,000 police and other law enforcement personnel there.

But the protests in the large Italian city were less unruly than last weekend, when looters ransacked businesses near the central Duomo area. Around 3,000 people rallied in Milan, with another smaller demonstration taking place in Rome.

As the day went on (and largely toward the end of demonstrations in many cities), clashes occurred between protesters and the authorities during the demonstrations across France.

The French interior ministry said it estimates 410,000 people to have taken part in protest throughout France today.

Demonstrations were set to take place in Paris and Marseille but protesters took to the streets in other cities for rallies like Lyon and Nantes.

There were reports about clashes between protesters and police in several cities, including Paris.

There were protests in the city of Lyon, in the east-central part of France, where police used tear gas to disperse protesters wearing masks.

There are also reports about clashes in Marseille, where police fired tear gas to disperse crowds.

About 550,000 people attended demonstrations throughout the country last weekend.

The mood over the past few days in France felt almost a bit apocalyptic. Business owners told me they were worried more looting might lie ahead, after gangs of individuals had ransacked and destroyed at least 3,000 shops across the country last weekend.

"Some of us are planning to buy weapons to defend ourselves, in case the pillagers come back. One day, there's going to be a tragedy — for sure," Jonathan Siad, owner of a tobacco shop in Paris, said to me.

Other store owners were too afraid to talk to us in front of the camera – they worried criminals might see the interview and target their shop.

Residents told me they would try to avoid the area where the demonstration was taking place. Only to add that they hoped the situation wouldn't escalate like last week, when even places far away from the actual marches became hotspots of clashes between the police and protesters.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez had admitted on Monday a "loss of control" last Saturday. The authorities thus increased the number of police deployed across France by 10,000 to 70,000 this Saturday.

First clashes between protesters and the police started to occur in the late afternoon in several cities across France such as Marseille, Lyon and Paris.

But for now, the much feared mass looting and ransacking doesn't seem to be happening. The situation is nowhere near the total chaos Paris and other cities like Marseille experienced last Saturday.

"Last weekend, our neighborhood resembled a war zone with gangs roaming the area. Today, it's completely empty apart from police with their vans," Yassaman Metghalchi, co-owner of a jewelry shop in the city center of Paris that got looted last Saturday, told me.

"All of our neighbors feel reassured – although the night is still young and we need to wait and see what will happen," she added.

Paris police say 110,000 protesters were on the streets in the city on Saturday. The anti-government "Yellow Vest" movementteamed up with aggrieved school students for this round of demonstrations.

The CGT trade union, meanwhile, said 800,000 participated in protests across France, with 250,000 people taking part in Paris.

Saturday's protesters were limited by Parisian authorities to the city's southeastern edge, away from the center.

Authorities prepared to help the protesters march safely from the Place d'Italie in the 13th arrondissement on the left bank of the Seine River to Porte de Vincennes which lies further away on the right bank.

A post on X by Paris Police Prefecture showed the Porte d'Italie from the sky ahead of the march.

French news agency AFP reported clashes in Paris after the demonstrations.

The French police used tear gas in response to protests in the southeastern city of Lyon. Use of tear gas was also reported in the cities of Lille, Toulouse and Nantes.

In Orleans, south of Paris, protesters also came out to the streets against a two-day congress held in the city of Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party.

According to polls, Le Pen is the frontrunner in France's presidential elections next year.
