#741. Juan Atkins Mourned By Fellow Artists: He ‘Sparked the Electronic Music Revolution We’re Living in Today’

The founding father of techno died on Oct. 31 at age 64.

The electronic music community is mourning the loss of Juan Atkins, a founding father of techno.

Atkins was found unresponsive in his hotel room in Mexico City on Saturday (Oct. 31) ahead of a scheduled performance at YuYu Cine Club, according to Resident Advisor. He was transported to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead shortly after arriving. He was 64.

Atkins made his name as part of the Belleville Three, the trio made up of him, Kevin Saunderson and Derrick May that’s widely credited for creating techno in 1980s Detroit. In this same era Atkins linked with fellow producer Richard Davis to form the electronic duo Cybotron. The group’s 1983 debut album, Enter, featured the futuristic “Clear,” which reached No. 52 on Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs on Oct. 8, 1983. The track ranked No. 77 on Billboard‘s list of the 100 Best Dance Songs of All Time and was also sampled on Missy Elliott’s Timbaland-produced 2005 hit “Lose Control.” Working under the Model 500 alias, Atkins’ “No UFO’s” reached No. 36 on Dance Singles Sales in 1985.

Beyond these highlights, Atkins’ catalog was not just vast but foundational, as he co-created and shaped a genre through his productions and live sets that took music at large further into the future. Decades-old Atkins productions still sound like they’ve come from deep space; it is work that has influenced, as fellow techno legend Kenny Larkin wrote in his remembrance, “every single one of you who does techno.”

Here, producers and event brands across the genre and beyond are remembering Atkins and his immeasurable influence.

The fellow Michigander shared an image of Atkins, writing, “Juan invented techno there is no debate, we lost another Black dance music innovator. It a devastating loss for Detroit and the techno community as a whole. My you find your cosmic cars in heaven.”

Fellow Detroit legend DJ Minx shared a photo of herself with Atkins, writing, “He taught us. He showed us the way. He put his heart into every beat dropped, every track produced. He gave us his all and I am forever grateful. He’s the reason I was the voice on WGPR’s Deep Space Radio. He supported and helped many, and I am thankful for him.

“The creator of Techno has left us with a gift that will be cherished for the rest of our lives,” she continued. “My condolences to his family and loved ones. I’m not sure what else to say right now. Rest in peace brother Juan. Your legacy will live on forever.”

“Heartbreaking news today. My brother Juan Atkins has passed away,” Kevin Saunderson, a fellow Belleville Three member, wrote on Instagram. “Juan was the originator of Techno, a true visionary who opened the door for so many of us, myself included. I’ll never forget how he showed me how to finish my first record, Triangle of Love. That meant a lot to me then, and it still does today.

“We shared a journey that changed music forever, and I’ll always be grateful for his friendship, guidance and everything he gave to our scene. My heart goes out to his family and loved ones. Rest in peace, Juan.”

The German techno legend shared an image of Atkins along with a long note reading “I can hardly believe this heartbreaking news. We have lost one of the true visionaries and founding fathers of electronic music. A pioneer who didn’t just create music but helped shape its future.

“With Cybotron, Model 500 and his legendary Metroplex label, Juan laid the foundations of what we know today as techno. His vision inspired generations and helped build a musical bridge between Detroit and Berlin, with Tresor becoming such an important part of that connection.

“Detroit always had a special place in my heart, and at our Omen club in Frankfurt, we always had our doors open to the Detroit pioneers and their extraordinary sound,” Väth continues. “That musical exchange was such an important part of our culture. Juan and I crossed paths many times over the decades, always with mutual respect, joy and a shared passion for music.

“His records have accompanied and inspired me since the early days. They remain part of my musical journey, and it meant a lot to me to include his music on my What I Used to Play compilation. Juan was truly ahead of his time. His unique fusion of futuristic sounds, soul, funk and electronic machines opened doors to an entirely new musical universe. My heart goes out to his family, loved ones, friends and fellow artists during this painful time.

“Dear Juan, your music, your vision and your spirit will live on. On our turntables, on our dancefloors and in our hearts. Thank you for opening the doors to the future. Rest in peace, dear Juan. With love, Sven.”

The fellow Detroit techno producer shared an image of himself with Atkins, writing, “Juan influenced every single one of you who does Techno. Directly or indirectly. No words to describe how devastating it is to lose Juan. As a kid, his music took me to space and beyond and eventually influenced and helped shape my life. RIP Juan Atkins.”

On Intagram, Tiga shared an image of him and Atkins with a five-minute voice note recounting the night Tiga saw Atkins play a set that he says did nothing less than alter his approach to electronic music.

“On December 31st, 1994 — New Year’s Eve — I was booked to play a party called Heaven in New York. I think it was actually in Queens. It was a big rave, 7,000 people. It was a huge deal at the time, and definitely a huge deal for me, because that was one of the first times I’d left Montreal to DJ at a big party.

“I played early — around 11 to midnight — and through some coincidence, Juan Atkins played after me. The party ended up getting shut down about an hour and a half after that, but it doesn’t matter. I got up there and I did my thing. I was a raver. I was into hardcore techno, hardcore breaks, UK stuff. It was crazy, and it went well.

“Then Juan came on, and he kind of blew my mind. To the point that I’m still here talking about it. The music blew my mind — he played incredible techno I had never really heard done like that before. But what really changed my whole outlook was that he had a little crew with him, maybe six friends from Detroit. And they didn’t look like us. They were kind of adults. They were really cool, and they were dancing — no socks on their heads, no lights, no weird gloves. Just cool-ass adults getting down.

“The combination of the music and watching his little posse groove — it was so cool and sexy and weird and legit that I was kind of transformed. After I handed over the decks, I just stood there and watched. I remember very clearly thinking: ‘I want some of that. Whatever they have going on, that little six-person nucleus — that’s what I want. Not the 3,000 ravers out there.’

“It was the first time Juan showed me something I didn’t even know was possible. A totally different energy profile. A totally different goal. The music was still techno — fast, powerful — but it was from the waist down. There was no kandi. It wasn’t built on rises and falls, on breakdowns. Nothing forced, nothing contrived. It was sexy and kind of deep, but still energetic.

“I didn’t really have the words for it then. I still don’t. I just know I’m still looking for that feeling. Every night I’m out there, I’m basically chasing what I felt watching Juan Atkins and his friends dance and play those records. It informed everything I did. It became the objective — what I strive for in the music I make, even though it obviously doesn’t sound like Detroit techno. The whole package: not giving a shit, thinking about the future, the optimism, the courage, being weird, reinventing sounds. It was just so cool.

“So I wanted to say thank you. It made a huge impression on me. We met a few times through the years, played together not that long ago in Mexico. Told jokes, talked s–t. He was an incredibly cool guy. That moment — it wasn’t so much his production. It was him as a DJ, what he represented. It gave me a target and changed how I looked at dance music. Changed how I look at techno. Period.

“One other thing I want to say: if you love someone’s music, if it touches you — just tell them. If you’re inspired by someone, tell them. Send a DM. Don’t be shy, don’t play it cool. Just tell each other when something really moves you.

“It’s important to recognize when something touches you. And being a musician is a pretty tough life. Making tracks is tough. A lot of the time, you don’t know the real reaction — you don’t always see it in front of you. Musicians’ lives have some crazy ups and downs, and you can find yourself years later wondering what the value was, or where you are. A lot of the time, the value is in how your music moves through the world. How it touches people. And if you have a chance to tell someone how it touched you — the journey it took, how it affected your life — just go for it.

“Thank you, Juan Atkins. For a million different things.”

The techno leader shared an image of Atkins, DJ Minx and himself on a golf cart, with a caption saying, “A quick spontaneous photo that I never imagined would be the last one – entering Movement Detroit earlier this year and running into DJ Minx and Atkins

“Juan imagined Techno before any of us,” Hawtin continues. “Without him, our music wouldn’t sound the way it does — if it existed at all. He welcomed a nerdy kid from Windsor into Techno Blvd with an encouraging smile and made me feel there was a place for me in a scene that was still being born. That moment changed my life. Thank you. My heart felt condolences to his family & friends.”

The techno icon shared an image of Atkins, writing “Cybotron. Model 500. Metroplex. The names alone suggested other worlds. The music transported me to faraway planets and galaxies, expanding my imagination and helping ignite the desire to pursue a life in music.

“Juan was pure inspiration. His imagination opened a universe of possibilities, and I’ll always be grateful for where it led me. Though we weren’t close, I cherish the chance encounters and meals we shared over the decades. I was always in awe of him. Farewell, Originator.”

The French producer shared an image of Atkins, writing, “I am profoundly saddened to hear the news about Juan. This is an immeasurable loss for the entire techno community. Juan’s music inspired and shaped my profound love for Detroit Techno. Today, we’ve lost one of the founding fathers of our music. All my thoughts are with Juan’s friends and family in Detroit and beyond.”

The Italian producer shared an image of himself with Atkins, writing “Respect and love for the originator, one of the founding fathers of techno music and a true visionary whose influence goes far beyond any genre. You changed the way we imagine and experience electronic music. Play his tracks today in his honor! Thank you for everything Juan. Juan Atkins. Model 500. Cybotron. Infiniti. Audio Tech …….. the list is long.”

The Instagram account for the fellow founders of electronic music shared an image of Kraftwerk co-founder Ralf Hütter with Atkins in Buenos Aires, Argentina in 2023.

The Instagram account for Detroit’s revered house and techno festival, which Atkins played with his Borderland project this past May, shared an image of Atkins with a caption that reads, “Juan Atkins sparked the electronic music revolution we’re living in today. Through Cybotron, he helped give the world a sound born from Detroit’s industrial grit. Iconic tracks like ‘Alleys of Your Mind’, ‘Clear’, and ‘Techno City’ were portals to a vision of what Detroit could sound like. And with Model 500, he pushed that vision forward, making music that was futuristic, soulful, and unmistakably Detroit.

“In his own words: ‘Nobody was calling it Techno music until I started calling it Techno music.’ Every generation of Detroit producers and DJs has built on the foundation he laid. Juan has been part of Movement’s story since its inception, taking the stage under his iconic aliases and projects, including Cybotron, Model 500, and most recently as Borderland at Movement 2026. Thank you, Juan, for the music and the vision.”

#740. Timbaland Sues Ex-Managers for $15M Over Accusations of ‘Financial Misconduct’

The veteran hitmaker claims his longtime manager and partner Gary Marella treated him like "a piggy bank" — accusations the manager strongly denies.

Timbaland is suing his former manager and business manager in a $15 million lawsuit that alleges the pair committed widespread misconduct in order to “enrich themselves” at the star’s expense.

The lawsuit, submitted Friday (Oct. 30) to a Los Angeles court and reviewed by Billboard, claims manager Gary Marella “stole millions in unauthorized commissions, fees, and reimbursements” and “falsified financial records” to conceal misdeeds.

The case also alleges that business manager Bruce Seckendorf caused big tax penalties by failing to pay federal taxes and also nearly caused the star’s house to be foreclosed, all while continuing to pay himself and Marella “millions” in fees.

“This is not a case about ordinary business losses or bookkeeping errors,” Timbaland’s lawyers write. “Defendants used their entrusted authority to enrich themselves and others, conceal financial misconduct, and deplete Timbaland’s valuable assets.”

In a response statement to Billboard on Monday (Nov. 2), Marella denied the lawsuit’s allegations, saying the “allegation that I paid myself without his knowledge is not true.”

“When I began managing Tim in 2017, long after he had produced his biggest hits, he was already in a bad financial place,” the manager said. “His financial problems did not begin with me. I came in to help rebuild his business. Over approximately nine years after I started working with Tim, we generated roughly $75 million in business.”

Timbaland (Timothy Zachery Mosley), a hit-making producer behind smash singles like Jay-Z’s “Big Pimpin’” and Justin Timberlake’s “SexyBack,” was managed for a decade by Marella, a veteran manager at Mono Music Group. That included Timbaland’s catalog sale to Hipgnosis Songs Fund in 2019, as well as his success with and later sale of Verzuz, a battle rap livestream series that spiked in popularity during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The discord between them first became public in August, when Timbaland lodged accusations against the manager as part of a wrongful termination lawsuit filed against the star by DJ E Feezy. In that filing, made in Florida state court, Timbaland blamed Marella for Feezy’s accusations, leveled allegations of financial impropriety and said he had terminated him as his manager more than a year earlier.

In Friday’s complaint, Timbaland doubled down on those accusations, claiming Marella had “treated plaintiff’s income and business ventures as his own checkbook.” The lawsuit claims Marella charged personal expenses to an American Express card, took improper compensation from both the Hipgnosis and Verzuz deals, and then covered his tracks with “falsified financial records” designed to “mislead” the star: “Defendants knew where the money went. Mosley did not.”

The lawsuit takes particular aim at their work on Beatclub, an online marketplace Timbaland and Marella co-founded in 2021 to help creators and producers monetize their beats and music. The producer’s attorneys say Marella “grossly mismanaged” the company and “treated Mosley as a piggy bank to repair the problems he created.”

“Marella depleted investor funds, spent company money contrary to how he represented it would be used, incurred obligations Beatclub could not pay, failed to pay employees and creators he hired, and spent money contrary to board restrictions,” the lawsuit claims. “Instead of disclosing his misconduct and correcting it, Marella repeatedly lied about Beatclub’s financial condition.”

In his response statement to Billboard, Marella disputed those accusations, saying the pair had together “hired a bad CTO who spent a significant amount of our capital, repeatedly missed deadlines, and ultimately failed to build the platform properly.”

“These setbacks created substantial financial challenges for the company,” Marella says. “Beatclub faced the challenges and setbacks that many startups experience. Those difficulties should not be confused with financial misconduct.”

Seckendorf, who has been named a Billboard Top Business Manager for several years running, was the star’s accountant from 1998 onward before also becoming his business manager in 2016, according to the lawsuit. Timbaland’s attorneys claim that move came in the wake of the star discovering “millions of dollars of misconduct” by his previous managers and looking for new advisors.

“Seckendorf presented himself as the person who already knew Mosley’s finances, could repair the damage, and would prevent the same thing from happening again,” Timbaland’s lawyers write in the court filings. “Instead, defendants recreated, and substantially worsened, the very circumstances that Mosley had trusted them to prevent.”

Seckendorf did not immediately return a request for comment on the accusations.

In technical legal terms, the lawsuit accuses both men of breach of fiduciary duty, fraudulent concealment and civil theft. It also accuses Marella specifically of fraud, breach of contract and misappropriation of his likeness, and accuses Seckendorf specifically of professional negligence and aiding and abetting a breach of fiduciary duty. It seeks at least $15 million in damages, as well as other monetary penalties and injunctions.

#739. How researchers debunked ‘race science’: ‘a triumph of scientific self-correction’

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

David Silverberg is a journalist based in Toronto, Canada.

Civil-rights activist W. E. B. Du Bois.Credit: Bettmann/Getty

The Ends of Race: The Rise and Fall of a Scientific Myth Geoffrey Galt Harpham Princeton University Press (2026)

Two stories about the history of science around race emerge from the nineteenth century. Each tugs at our attention in a different way. Humanities scholar Geoffrey Galt Harpham chronicles them in a book with enthralling detail.

The Ends of Race tracks the decades spent by scientists and scholars intending to prove that human races were distinct, using methods such as measuring skulls and facial forms to set them in biologically fixed categories and develop taxonomies to rank humanity.

Why Africans should be telling the story of human origins

Why Africans should be telling the story of human origins

The first set of protagonists, including US anthropologist Josiah Nott and French anthropologist Julien-Joseph Virey, likened Black people’s skulls to ape skulls with evidence as threadbare as a spiderweb, intentionally pushing Black people down the ladder of desirable cultures. It was a myth born to provide cover for racism, Harpham writes.

The second story starts in 1900, during a tide-turning moment for science. Scholars began publishing studies countering the oppressive theories of race scientists. Ultimately, the discrediting of the concept of biological race emerged as a triumph of scientific self-correction.

These stories serve as a potent reminder of not just how science can get it so wrong, but how flawed research can eventually be quashed by sensible approaches. In the case of race, inaccuracies were sustained solely by political and social ends.

As with any good story, the author confidently guides us through a heady mix of characters. And Harpham even contends that this tragic era in science offers a happy ending. Once natural science had dismissed race as a biological reality, authors such as W. E. B. Du Bois took the opportunity to reframe race as a social and cultural identity, to invite solidarity among Black people.

The scientific muddling of race and species, and its lasting effect on perpetuating division, has its roots with Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus. His 1735 book Systema Naturae categorized every kind of organism, a magnificent feat at the time. But this process encouraged questions about divisions among humans, similar to what Linnaeus saw in other species.

This area of research excited the scientific community. Early race theorists, such as Nott, clamoured for the “magnificent opportunity to establish the ability of empirical research and scientific method to engage with issues whose interest and importance could be immediately grasped by the public and even valued by the state”, Harpham writes.

Physician Petrus Camper proposed that the angle between the jaw and forehead could differentiate species, a theory used in scientific racism. Credit: Antiqua Print Gallery/Alamy

Nott took Linneaus’s categorization a step further, arguing that human races were not just environmental varieties of a single family, but separate, fixed species created independently by God. He thought that interbreeding between “remote” races led to weak, disease-prone and infertile offspring, and applied mortality data to his claim that Black people in the United States enjoyed joyous lives under Southern chattel slavery but perished in freedom in cold Northern cities.

You can imagine Harpham’s eyes rolling when he shares Nott’s racist views, but he recognizes that these ideas weren’t just the provenance of one man. US physician Samuel George Morton published work in the 1830s in which he expanded on his theory that skull size and shape reflected brain size and intellectual capacity. He ranked racial cultures on their mean cranial size: Caucasians at the number-one position, followed by Mongolians, Malays, Native Americans and Ethiopians (a catch-all term for Black people) at the bottom.

How ‘organized looting and plunder’ drove Britain’s second scientific revolution

How ‘organized looting and plunder’ drove Britain’s second scientific revolution

The context of slavery is necessary to fully understand some of these outlandish studies, Harpham stresses. Both Nott and Morton argued that since the time of ancient Egypt, enslaver–enslaved relationships and the physical racial features of each of these groups had remained unchanged, pointing to racial hierarchies laid out as permanent laws of nature rather than temporary social conceptions. At the time, there was little pushback. After all, enslavers benefited from these notions.

#737. Tate McRae’s ‘Housewife’ Scores Second Week at No. 1 on Billboard Global Charts

Plus, first top 10s for Jamie Miller and Felipe & Rodrigo.

Tate McRae’s “Housewife” adds a second week at No. 1 on both the Billboard Global 200 and Billboard Global Excl. U.S., a week after it debuted at the summit of both surveys.

The song remains the biggest hit in the world with 64.1 million streams (up 15%) and 3,000 sold (down 52%) globally Oct. 23-29, according to Luminate. It totaled 44.2 million streams (up 32%) outside the U.S.

“Housewife” became the Canadian singer-songwriter’s second leader on each chart, and her first to debut on top. “Greedy” ruled the Global 200 for two weeks and Global Excl. U.S. for five in 2023-24.

Elsewhere in the Global 200’s top five, Karol G, Judeline and rusowsky’s “BbY WOW” rebounds 3-2 after six weeks at No. 1 since September; ADÉLA’s “Nicole Kidman” rises 4-3, off its No. 2 best; Olivia Rodrigo and Chappell Roan’s “Expectations” drops to No. 4 from its No. 2 peak; and Ashe’s “Stop the Wedding!” jumps 10-5 for a new high.

The Global Excl. U.S. top five is rounded by “BbY WOW,” which holds at No. 2, likewise after six weeks at No. 1 since September; “Nicole Kidman,” up 5-3 after reaching No. 2; “Expectations,” which keeps at its No. 4 high; and A2O LITE’s “Neon,” down to No. 5 from its No. 3 peak.

Jamie Miller earns his first top 10 on both the Global 200, where “Babydoll” bounds 37-10, and Global Excl. U.S., surging 31-9. The pop single by the Welsh artist, which he co-wrote, drew 19.8 million streams (up 36%) and sold 13,000 (up 55%) worldwide in the tracking week. It also notches a second week at No. 1 on the U.K.’s Official Singles Chart.

Plus, Felipe & Rodrigo, from Brazil, achieve their first Global Excl. U.S. top 10 as “Pos (Em Brasilia)” pushes 16-10 with 18.7 million streams (up 8%) outside the U.S.

The Billboard Global 200 and Global Excl. U.S. charts rank songs based on streaming and sales activity culled from more than 200 territories around the world, as compiled by Luminate. The Global 200 is inclusive of worldwide data and the Global Excl. U.S. chart comprises data from territories excluding the United States.

Chart ranks are based on a weighted formula incorporating official-only streams on both subscription and ad-supported tiers of audio and video music services, as well as download sales, the latter of which reflect purchases from full-service digital music retailers from around the world, with sales from direct-to-consumer (D2C) sites excluded from the charts’ calculations.

The latest charts, dated Nov. 7, 2026, will update on Billboard.com tomorrow, Nov. 3. For both tallies, the top 100 titles are available to all readers on Billboard.com, while the complete 200-title rankings are visible on Billboard Pro, Billboard’s subscription-based service. #736. Roku Sees Soaring Sales, Net Income of $183M, As It Blasts Past Analyst Expectations

The move comes as Roku awaits the close of its acquisition by Fox.

Roku blew past third-quarter earnings expectations as it gears up for its pending acquisition by Fox.

The streaming platform reported net revenue of $1.5 billion, up 24 percent year-over-year and above analyst expectations of $1.41 billion. The company said the third quarter was the highest year-over-year revenue growth for its media and entertainment vertical in four years “as media companies invested on the Roku platform to promote their content and services.”

Net income was $183 million, up an eye-popping 639 percent from a year earlier, which translates to diluted earnings per share of $1.20. Analysts had predicted earnings per share of $0.55, according to the Zaks consensus.

Platform revenue was $1.3 billion, up 34 percent year-over-year, driven by increases in both advertising and subscriptions. Streaming hours were 39.9 billion, up 9 percent.

Advertising revenue grew 23 percent year-over-year to $727 million, marking Roku’s ninth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth. This was helped by a shift to higher margin ad products, as well as strong results in political advertising. Roku said political advertising on the platform in the third quarter exceeded the comparable quarter from the 2024 U.S. presidential election cycle.

Subscriptions revenue also grew 23 percent year-over-year to $581 million, with gross margin of 40.9 percent, down roughly 180 basis points due to a “strategic mix shift toward premium subscriptions.” Overall revenue grew as Roku pointed to its completed rollout of the new U.S. home screen, which has improved content recommendations.

“One early result we are seeing is a reduction in Premium Subscription cancellations,” the Roku shareholder letter reads. The company is now rolling out the new home screen to international markets.

The earnings come after Fox announced in June an agreement to acquire Roku for $160 per share in a cash and Fox Class A common stock transaction valuing Roku at $22 billion. The deal, which combines Fox’s sports, news and entertainment content and the Tubi streaming service with Roku’s connected TV platform, The Roku Channel and more, follows a strategic review by Roku, which chose Fox as the preferred bidder.

In June, Roku CEO Anthony Wood called the deal a “great price.” “Put simply, it’s the best way to accelerate our long-term strategy and continue shaping the future of television,” he said at the time.

Fox reported earnings Monday, with CEO Lachlan Murdoch saying Fox is working “constructively” with the Department of Justice to close its deal for Roku. The transaction has already been approved by shareholders and foreign regulatory bodies.

Due to the pending transaction, Roku said it would not provide a financial outlook, nor did it host an earnings call Monday. The company also did not provide a financial outlook last quarter.

“We remain on track for the second-half 2026 forecast we provided in the proxy statement, and our pending acquisition by Fox is an extraordinary opportunity to accelerate our vision, allowing us to scale faster and innovate more aggressively for viewers, partners and advertisers,” Wood said in the letter.

#735. Taylor Swift’s Songs Written for Movies, Ranked (Critic’s Picks)

Swift's soundtrack credits include Cats, The Hunger Games, Where the Crawdads Sing and more.

Taylor Swift is known for lending her talents to other artists — but the pop star has also shared plenty of original songs to some of your favorite movies.

Swift has appeared in several films: Amsterdam, Cats, The Giver, Valentine’s Day, and Hannah Montana: The Movie – the latter as herself. She even made a cameo on the Fox series New Girl.

Along with appearing in those films, the superstar has written songs for a few of them as well: She crafted two tracks from the Hannah Montana: The Movie soundtrack, one for Valentine’s Day, and one for Cats. Swift has also penned tracks for films she didn’t appear in, including two for the original Hunger Games, one for Britain’s Got Talent winner Paul Potts’ biopic One Chance, one for Fifty Shades Darker, one for her own documentary Miss Americana and one for Where the Crawdads Sing.

Blending her usual genres of country and pop, certain tracks were written directly for the films like “Beautiful Ghosts” and “Safe & Sound,” while others — like “Today Was a Fairytale” — she had in her vault and offered up for soundtracks. “I wrote that song last summer, and when this movie opportunity came about, I reached back into my pocket and thought, ‘I think this is perfect for the soundtrack. I hope it’s perfect for the soundtrack,’” she told The Tennessean back in 2010 of the Valentine’s Day song.

“Today Was a Fairytale” and “I Don’t Wanna Live Forever” with former One Direction member ZAYN both reached No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100, but her highest peak on the chart with a soundtrack cut came in the summer of 2026, when “I Knew It, I Knew You” — created for the Toy Story 5 end credits — debuted at No. 1. In honor of her ever-expanding catalog of music written for the big screen, keep reading to see Billboard‘s ranking of all the songs Swift has made for movies below.

Now a cult favorite, the silver screen version of Cats wasn’t warmly received by critics or the general public – but Swift’s song with legendary composer Andrew Lloyd Webber did earn a Golden Globe nomination for Best Original Song as well as a Grammy nod for Best Song Written for Visual Media.

Movie: Hannah Montana: The MovieYear: 2009Hot 100 Peak: 17

Swift cameos in the film to perform the twangy and dreamy ditty that chronicles falling in love. “You showed me somethin’ that I couldn’t see / You opened my eyes and you made me believe,” she sings in her Nashville peal.

Movie: Valentine’s DayYear: 2010Hot 100 Peak: 2

Another fitting track for a film about the both the happiness and the perils of romance. “Today Was a Fairytale” perfectly evokes the feelings of the first flush of a young relationship. And in Swift’s case, works with her character’s happy ending (as far as high school goes). (She would later re-record the song for Fearless (Taylor’s Version) in 2021.)

Movie: Hannah Montana: The MovieYear: 2009Hot 100 Peak: N/A

The only song that Swift doesn’t perform on this list, Miley Cyrus’ Hannah Montana stands in as lead vocalist in the fun and exuberant tune about knowing “exactly who you are.”

Movie: The Hunger GamesYear: 2012Hot 100 Peak: 19In the midst of her sonic evolution that started with 2012’s Red, Swift goes into almost full rock mode for The Hunger Games in this taste of her talents across all genres.

Movie: One ChanceYear: 2013Hot 100 Peak: 24Before there was 1989, there was “Sweeter Than Fiction,” a splashy, electro-pop anthem that became the nascence of her work partnership with Jack Antonoff, as it’s the first song they co-wrote and co-produced together.

Movie: Where the Crawdads SingYear: 2022Hot 100 Peak: 60

Appropriately cinematic and atmospherically eerie, Swift takes on the mysterious story of a girl who grew up in North Carolina in the cut co-produced by Aaron Dessner.

Movie: Miss AmericanaYear: 2020Hot 100 Peak: 50

Released along with her 2020 documentary that chronicled her life at the time – and partially detailed Swift’s frustration at her lack of political outspokenness – “Only the Young” proffers a thumping and hopeful message to the younger generations about picking up the mantle of activism. “They aren’t gonna help us / Too busy helping themselves / They aren’t gonna change this / We gotta do it ourselves,” she sings.

Movie: Fifty Shades Darker Year: 2017Hot 100 Peak: 2Sexy, sensual and full of longing, the collaboration between Swift and ZAYN fuses pop and R&B in glamorous fashion. “I gave you somethin’, but you gave me nothin’ / What is happening to me?” Swift cries on the bold confessional.

Movie: Toy Story 5Year: 2026Hot 100 Peak: 1 (two weeks)

Written in just a few hours after Swift saw an early screening of Toy Story 5, “I Knew It, I Knew You” finds the star singing from the perspective of cowgirl Jessie as she grapples with her greater purpose. Accentuated by harmonica and rootsy chord progressions, the track marks a return to form of sorts for Swift as she experimented again with the country influences she cut her teeth on, making the nostalgia factor of the end-credits track even more powerful.

Movie: The Hunger GamesYear: 2012Hot 100 Peak: 30

A magnum opus of folk balladry, the trio of Swift and The Civil Wars’ Joy Williams and John Paul White tender beautifully sparse harmonies in the Grammy winner for Best Song Written for Visual Media. Emotively unfettered, “Safe & Sound” mystically blends indie-pop sensibilities with the sounds of Katniss Everdeen’s Appalachian home, ultimately crafting a delicate and raw showcase for Swift, Williams and White.

#733. Bruce Springsteen Backs Michigan’s Dr. Abdul El-Sayed for U.S. Senate Amid Haley Stevens Reversal: ‘He’s a Fighter’

"I'm in his corner 100%," the Boss said of the Democratic nominee.

Bruce Springsteen has shared his thoughts on the race in Michigan for U.S. Senate, backing Dr. Abdul El-Sayed for the seat as Election Day draws nearer.

In a Monday (Nov. 2) post on Instagram, The Boss shared a statement explaining why he supports the Democratic nominee. “Dr. El-Sayed is a fighter for our American Constitution,” Springsteen wrote. “He’s a fighter for our American Democracy, and he’s a fighter against the corrupt, lawless, and anti-American leadership currently in the White House.”

The musician added, “I’m in his corner 100%.”

The endorsement comes amid a close race in Michigan between Dr. El-Sayed and his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, to take over Democrat Gary Peters’ seat in the Senate. A Democratic win in Michigan is crucial for Democrats as they work to flip the Senate, and recently, Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens threw everyone a curveball by rescinding her support of Dr. El-Sayed and endorsing Rogers. As a result, the state’s Democratic Party chairman Curtis Hertel announced on X that Stevens “is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.”

Springsteen has long been vocal in his political opinions, especially in recent years. He’s repeatedly spoken out against Donald Trump in particular, which has led the president to publicly take aim at the Rock & Roll Hall of Famer a number of times — not that it’s had any success in silencing the Boss.

“I do what I want to do,” Springsteen — who’s topped the Billboard 200 11 times over the course of his career — told Rolling Stone of using his recent Land of Hopes & Dreams trek as a political statement. “This was the show I wanted to make, the story I wanted to tell … I’m sure there were people, and I’ve read things where people were vehement about the content of the show. And that’s just the way the chips fall.”

#732. Former ‘Ellen’ Executive Producer Matthew Wright Dies as Ellen DeGeneres Posts Tearful Video Calling Him “The Glue to Our Entire Family”

Former The Ellen DeGeneres Show executive producer Matthew Wright died Friday in what a GoFundMe campaign for his family calls an “unfathomable tragedy.” He was 52, according to reports.

Wright died while working remotely in Los Angeles, according to the GoFundMe, while his family is in New York. Both Wright and his husband were “laid off this summer,” the GoFundMe states.

“And the unexpected costs of getting Matt home, a funeral and a memorial are impossible for the family to bear,” the GoFundMe reads. “If Matt has ever made you laugh, said an encouraging word right when you needed it or ordered one too many appetizers for the enjoyment of the whole table, now is the time to repay the favor. Please donate what you can and share this with anyone who’s been in the orbit of Matt’s huge heart. DeGeneres posted a tearful video on Instagram Monday remembering Wright, who worked on her show from 2006 to its finale in 2022.

“We are all in shock. He gave that same depth of love to his friendships. My heart breaks for his husband, Justin, his family, and all of us who loved him. I was so lucky to work beside Matt for so many years and to call him my friend. We should have had so much more time with him.”

Former The Real co-host Loni Love also paid tribute to Wright, writing on Facebook that she was “devastated and heartbroken” to hear that he died.

“He was such a talented, sweet man and always game for anything. I cannot believe he’s gone,” she wrote. “What a pleasure it was to have known him. Sending love and heartfelt condolences to his husband, family and all who loved him.”

The fundraising post, which sought to raise $50,000 for a funeral and memorial as well as a trust for his niece, had already surpassed its goal by Monday afternoon.

#729. From rotten food to political opponents: Researchers explore how disgust relates to our beliefs, and why the connection is complicated

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But ahead of the US midterm elections, does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But ahead of the US midterm elections, does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate, even political opponents can become objects of disgust.

Psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.

"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada, told DW.

But disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale, developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:

One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.

Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on new experiences.

"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side, and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.

Indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe."

Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.

"We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar said.

Disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.

A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.

Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in US politics, reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats, reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.

However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.

Some early studies suggested conservatives showed stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam, struggled to reproduce those findings.

Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.

"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London, told DW.

Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.

Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.

"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it."

The researchers surveyed 632 US adults, asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility."

They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.

But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.

What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.

"People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he said.

Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.

He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.

Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.

"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar said.

The new study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.

Inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best."

Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.

"I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he said, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.

Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he said.

The research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.

"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.

Inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance. "The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he said.

"It's one of the many influences on people's politics."

Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.

He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.

"Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he said. Edited by: Rosalie Delaney

#728. Justin Timberlake to Release 4-Part Docuseries That Includes Janet Jackson as a Guest

The project is set to arrive on Apple TV by the end of the year.

Justin Timberlake has some things to get off his chest. Variety reported Monday (Nov. 2) that the pop star has a four-part “tell-all” docuseries in the works at Apple TV, featuring none other than Janet Jackson as a guest.

The project is reportedly expected to arrive on the streamer in December, with no further details available at press time aside from one of the discussion topics that will be included. With Miss Jackson onboard, the doc will almost certainly look back on the pair’s infamous 2004 Super Bowl controversy, which involved Timberlake exposing her breast on live TV — aka the incident from which the term “wardrobe malfunction” was born.

Billboard has reached out to Timberlake’s reps for comment.

The project comes amid a reflective chapter for the former *NSYNC boy bander, who made headlines in 2021 with a public apology to Jackson acknowledging the disparity in how they were respectively treated after the Super Bowl controversy. “I am deeply sorry for the times in my life where my actions contributed to the problem, where I spoke out of turn, or did not speak up for what was right,” Timberlake wrote. “I understand that I fell short in these moments and in many others and benefited from a system that condones misogyny and racism.”

Also in his apology, Timberlake expressed remorse for the disrespectful ways in which he’d previously spoken about Britney Spears following their breakup in 2002.

Things got rocky for JT a few years later in 2024, when he was arrested on suspicion of driving while intoxicated in the Hamptons. He ultimately pleaded guilty to a lesser impaired-driving charge, and the singer was sentenced to 25 hours of community service.

“It’s been a tough week,” Timberlake told fans at one of his Forget Tomorrow World Tour concerts shortly afterward. “I know I’m hard to love sometimes, but you keep loving me right back.”

After the trek ended the following year, the star revealed another challenge he’d been facing behind the scenes: Lyme disease.

“Living with this can be relentlessly debilitating, both mentally and physically,” he wrote in a statement at the time. “When I first got the diagnosis I was shocked for sure. But, at least I could understand why I would be onstage and in a massive amount of nerve pain or, just feeling crazy fatigue or sickness.”

Timberlake hasn’t dropped an album since 2024, reaching No. 4 on the Billboard 200 with Everything I Thought It Was. He did, however, recently team up with Quavo on the new song “House Music,” which dropped in early October.

#725. American Airlines hikes annual fees on rewards cards for first time since 2018

American Airlines is raising the annual fee for two of its rewards credit cards for the first time since 2018 and adding new benefits like a TSA PreCheck credit and points from spending on hotels.

The fee on the Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select World Elite Mastercard will go up to $150 a year from $99. That is the first hike since 2018, when it raised the fee from $95 to $99, an airline spokeswoman said.

The Citi AAdvantage Business Mastercard will also have a fee increase and will now cost $150 a year.

Airlines and their bank partners have been steadily raising fees on rewards credit cards.

Those cards generate billions of dollars a year for airlines, which make money when miles are sold to banks, which then give them to customers. American's move, announced Tuesday, follows similar increases by rivals such as United Airlines.

Meanwhile, American Express last year raised the fee on its popular Platinum card, which comes with airport lounge access, to $895 a year from $695. JPMorgan Chase increased the annual fee on its competing card, the Sapphire Reserve, to $795 from $550.

The new perks for the American card include three times AAdvantage miles earnings on hotels booked through American's portal, a credit of up to $120 every four years for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck, and a $100 annual statement credit on in-flight purchases like food.

#724. Can Democrats Really Flip the Senate? Hollywood Holds Its Breath

What the odds really look like as a largely liberal industry frets in commissaries, Zooms and boardrooms.

Months of election drama will finally come to an end Tuesday as voters across America head to the polls. Like a Game of Thrones series finally working to the finale, hopefully with a less divisive resolution.

The will-they-or-won’t-they saga has been more intense than pretty much anything else onscreen this season (well, except for You Can See Everything, of course). Hollywood — at least judging from the fundraising efforts by major entertainment world figures for Democratic candidates in Texas, Georgia, Florida and elsewhere — has a vested interest in getting a Democratic flip in both chambers of Congress.

So does it happen?The House seems almost surely headed for a Democratic handover — the party needs to flip only three seats, and well over a dozen Republican seats are in polling trouble. A blue wave, or at least strong ripple, on that side. (High Democratic turnout in early voting is further encouraging for the party’s prospects.) But the Senate, where Democrats need to flip four of the 22 Republican seats up for reelection while holding all 13 of their own (or flip five if they lose one), seems a far murkier prospect.Right now, Republicans are behind at the polls in at least eight races where they currently hold seats. Obvious flip, right? Not so fast. The Trump era has been defined by Republican undercounting in pre-election polling, which could make some of the Democratic leads illusory, though midterm polls tend to be more accurate. (MAGA supporters — those least likely to respond to polls — tend not to come out as much for midterm races, making their non-responses less impactful.)That undercount makes very close races in Alaska, Maine and Iowa a lot more likely to break for Republicans. That’s especially true in Alaska, where recent backlash over Sullivan-gate — i.e., the alleged orchestration by the campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola to get a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot and potentially confuse supporters over the Republican nominee of the same name — could tip the election to the GOP. The Republican candidates in Maine and Iowa, meanwhile, have high likability ratings among voters.Democrats do seem to have more sizable edges in Texas, Ohio and North Carolina, making those likely if not certain to turn blue. North Carolina’s Democratic Roy Cooper is firmly in control, Texas’ James Talarico has widened his advantage in recent days over Ken Paxton, and former Sen. Sherrod Brown has begun to open a clear if narrow advantage over Jon Husted, in the job only two years as J.D. Vance’s replacement.That still means Democrats will have to pull off one more flip, and it’s unclear where that comes from. Kansas is perhaps the best bet, with the moderate Democratic pastor Rev. Adam Hamilton putting some daylight between himself and incumbent Roger Marshall. And Marshall is unpopular — but then Kansas hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since the Great Depression (or, in movie terms, the year Grand Hotel won best picture).An X factor is South Carolina, which historically has been more red than Elmo but now faces some chaos with the candidacy of political newbie Darline Graham, sister of late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who has been seen as a nepotistic choice by voters in some polls. That could open the door to her pediatrician challenger, Annie Andrews, until a few months ago thought a lost cause.If either Kansas or South Carolina go Dems’ way — and honestly had you raised that possibility six months ago, people would have thought you were Sarah Connor-level crazy — attention then turns to the Democrats trying to defend their contested seats. While that seems likely in previously in-play races in Minnesota, Georgia and New Hampshire, such a prospect is more uncertain in Michigan, where Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, facing a stunning Democratic mutiny from former primary challenger Haley Stevens, could see some moderates bleed to his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers. Should El-Sayed surprisingly not win the race — and, to be clear, with a five-point poll lead, the smart money is still with him — then Dems would need an additional flip beyond the targeted four.Still, even if they don’t get it and the Senate ends up 50-50 (and decided by the vice president), it could hamper the GOP agenda, since such a count opens up the possibility of peeling any single Republican from the caucus to block a vote. (Democrats refer to this as Joe Manchin Syndrome.)Democrats could take heart in one possible major blue-red reversal — but it’s not in the Senate. Florida hasn’t elected a Democratic governor in 32 years. But David Jolly is within a few points of the Trump-endorsed Byron Donalds, and the idea of a Democrat — even one who not that long ago was a Republican — replacing Ron DeSantis in the country’s third most-populous state would certainly add some thickener to the stew.What’s at stake for Democrats and the many in Hollywood who support them? A bulwark against Donald Trump, for starters, but also a rare chance to control both chambers over the next term. The party has been able to do that only once in the past 16 years and only three times since 1994. Before then, it happened regularly — that 1994 election and its famous “Contract With America” Gingrichian revolution ended eight straight years of Democrats controlling both bodies.Of course, who remembers that? You’d have to have been working in Hollywood when the first Lion King came out to harbor such a memory. A Senate majority rises and falls like the sun.

Imagine Entertainment and Weed Road are developing a series based on the 2011 book by Daniel H. Wilson, with Imagine’s Ron Howard attached to direct the pilot and Weed Road’s Akiva Goldsman set to showrun and write the pilot. No network or streamer is yet involved.

Brilliantly conceived and amazingly detailed, Robopocalypse is an action-packed epic with chilling implications about the real technology that surrounds us.”

“Robopocalypse has all the scale and suspense of a major action story, but what drew me to it are the thought-provoking themes and humanity at its center,” said Howard in a statement. “Daniel created a future that feels both startling and increasingly plausible, with characters who must figure out what connects us when the technology we rely on turns against us. I am also thrilled to work with Akiva again. We have shared some incredibly meaningful creative experiences, and this feels like the right story to bring us back together.”

Howard and Goldsman are longtime collaborators, dating back to the film A Beautiful Mind, which won Howard best director and best picture Oscars, and nabbed Goldsman the best adapted screenplay statue. They also spent time developing another popular project for the screen, Stephen King’s Dark Tower, which became a movie and had designs to spinoff into a TV show that didn’t come to fruition.

#721. In Indonesia, PhD students blow the whistle on bad supervision

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

PhD students at Indonesian universities say that the quality of supervision in the nation is often poor, and that many supervisors engage in inappropriate behaviour.Credit: epsgalery85/Shutterstock

When Rully Charitas Prahmana went to the United States as a visiting lecturer, the academic culture shock was extreme. “I was surprised to see an academic supervisor go cycling with his PhD students on the weekend,” says Prahmana, a mathematics lecturer at Ahmad Dahlan University in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, and a visiting researcher at the Western Michigan University in Kalamazoo.

Prahmana can’t imagine that kind of interaction at home, describing himself as being in the minority for occasionally holding informal discussions with students in a warung, small street-food stalls or restaurants that are common across Indonesia. Many of his colleagues never meet their students in casual settings, he says.

PhD candidate–supervisor relationships in the southeast Asian archipelago nation are often less centred around direct scientific supervision in a laboratory or throughout a research project than in much of the rest of the world’s PhD programmes. Many early-career researchers instead say that they only meet supervisors for brief formal discussions, to sign research proposals, or to sign off on their dissertations. Students at larger and more prestigious institutions sometimes have more direct supervision, but “mostly, what we have is power asymmetry”, says Prahmana.

“I met my supervisors routinely but instead of supervising me, they were gossiping about other lecturers,” says one of 11 PhD students interviewed for this article. Several individuals requested anonymity to protect their careers.

Some described being asked to take on tasks at personal expense. One interviewee, for example, said that she had to pay for access to sampling sites before doing her wet-lab research. “I need to take out 200,000 rupiah [around US$12] every week for a year per sampling site,” says the student. All told, she was spending around $1,700 a year on her sampling work. The average monthly salary in Indonesia is around $200.

“I am sure there are many professors who treat students unfairly,” says an anonymous student in Semarang, Indonesia.

“But we are forced to accept what our supervisors say because we just want to graduate soon,” says another.

Some young academics argue that the problem of bad supervisors stems from poor management of PhD programmes in Indonesia, which aims to increase its population of doctoral graduates from around 75,000 to 125,000 by 2045. Brian Yuliarto, the nation’s minister for higher education, science and technology, says that this ambition will drive economic growth. National statistical data are patchy, with broad censuses every ten years, but Indonesia has an estimated 64 million people between the ages of 16 and 30. Yuliarto describes this group — 22% of the country’s population — as “a demography bonus”, telling Nature that the nation needs “to transform them into highly qualified human resources”.

Today in Indonesia, there are 272 PhD holders per one million people, compared with around 14,000 per million in the United States, for example.

My relationship with my PhD supervisor has become toxic — what do I do?

My relationship with my PhD supervisor has become toxic — what do I do?

To boost this number, the Indonesia Endowment Fund for Education, an agency that manages the country’s $9.1-million fund, has set aside money for another 2,500 PhD scholarships this year, says Yuliarto. Nearly half of these will be for those who want to pursue PhD opportunities overseas; the rest will be reserved for people studying partially or fully in Indonesia.

But only some Indonesian universities are set up to provide enough supervision to double the number of people graduating with high-quality PhDs, argues Berry Juliandi, dean of mathematics and natural sciences at IPB University in Bogor. He says that the new funding isn’t supported by strategic policies and regulations around improving academic supervision for the nation’s universities, which will therefore not be able to deliver a high-quality PhD experience.

Indonesia has 4,303 higher-education institutions. The country’s National Accreditation Agency for Higher Education counts only 226 of those as ‘highly qualified’, a criterion that accounts for the quality of not only the physical infrastructure, but also scientific prestige and experience and the teaching skills of the lecturers at the institutions.

Even at these institutions, conflicts between supervisors and PhD students are rife, says Fikri Yanda, a PhD student at Walailak University in Thai Buri, Thailand, who manages the ‘pembela_mahasiswa_indonesia’ (‘Indonesia student advocates’) Instagram account, which discusses academia in Indonesia.

Rully Charitas Prahmana, who teaches mathematics at Ahmad Dahlan University, in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, says that there is often a power asymmetry between PhD supervisors and students in Indonesia.Credit: Rully Charitas Indra Prahmana

So far this year, Indonesia’s ministry of education has reported 874 cases of inappropriate behaviour, including ethical misconduct, violence, sexual harassment and abuse of power.

This kind of behaviour “hampers our freedom to think freely as academics”, says Andik Wijayanto, a biology PhD student at Gadjah Mada University in Yogyakarta, because scientists aren’t able to challenge the status quo. Many students are afraid to make mistakes, he says. (Wijayanto, who also lectures in biology at the State University of Malang in East Java, says that he doesn’t have any problems with his own supervisors.)

In 2017, Indonesia’s higher-education ministry found that of 5,366 professors in Indonesia, 3,800 had not published peer-reviewed papers in international journals that the government considered reputable. This led to stricter regulations that now require all professors and other university lecturers with master’s and doctoral degrees of all disciplines to publish in high-quality Scopus-indexed journals. But the policy backfired: some academics were snared by predatory journals — organizations that offer to publish papers for a fee, often using aggressive or misleading solicitation practices, while not providing legitimate peer review or adequate editorial assistance. Other researchers manipulated their citation indexes to achieve high performance scores in the government’s evaluation system.

In 2021, the ministry introduced a regulation on scientific integrity that sanctions scientists who engage in data fabrication, plagiarism and forged authorship. This was followed by another regulation signed by Yuliarto this February, which asks institutions to assess ‘scientific integrity’ when evaluating university lecturers’ performance, a determining factor for their career opportunities.

#720. With ‘The Girl of Your Dreams,’ Ashe Finds Her Sweet Spot: “I’m A Really Solid Version of Myself”

The pop singer's viral hit "Stop The Wedding!" continues to climb the Billboard Hot 100, reaching its highest peak yet this week with the top 25 in sight.

Ashe is tucked away in her Nashville home. It’s more of a cottage, she explains, a cup of coffee in hand. It’s straight out of The Holiday.

“It looks like a grandma decorated it,” the singer-songwriter tells The Hollywood Reporter on a recent Zoom call. “But it was in fact me.”

The 33-year-old is in the midst of a career-high. Her latest album, The Girl of Your Dreams, has earned the singer her highest Billboard 200 debut to date, landing at No. 20. The album’s pre-release single “Stop The Wedding!” has continued to climb the charts, landing at its highest-yet position at No. 28. Related Stories News Lenny Kravitz Debunks Viral Rumor That He Died in Horrific Learjet Plane Crash Music Marty Erlichman, Barbra Streisand's Longtime Manager, Dies at 97

It’s not the first time she’s experienced a viral moment — her 2019 single “Moral of the Story,” which was featured in Netflix’s To All The Boys I’ve Loved Before: P.S. I Still Love You, served as a breakout moment for the singer. Heading into the album, she was hopeful that the hype surrounding “Stop The Wedding!” would push people to listen to the entire album, which given its debut this week, it seems that came to fruition.

“‘Stop The Wedding!’ while to the world it stands alone and on its own little island, to me, it’s No. 1 of 11 songs,” she explains. “It lives in a body of work. I’m excited for people to have that context.”

There was a time for Ashe, whose real name is Ashlyn Rae Willson, when she felt extremely protective with her work. There’s always a complicated feeling when sharing an album with the world. But lately, thanks to her latest album and her 2025 stint as The Favors with collaborator Finneas, she’s finding herself moving away from that.

“A previous version of a previous songwriter that I was, was a bit more precious,” she says. “Now, as I’ve gotten older, it’s not that I wouldn’t take it less serious, but it’s art. It’s meant to be interpreted and perceived and misinterpreted.”

Adds Ashe: “I’m very OK with that — probably in a way that I didn’t used to be. I can’t wait for people who love it to love it. And for people that it’s not for, to not get it, and it just to be here.”

When did you notice something was happening with “Stop The Wedding!” and its rising viral moment?

I was on tour with Benson Boone when I started teasing “Stop The Wedding!” It came out while I was on that tour. I was able to feel the difference of that song pretty immediately. A couple days after it came out, I played it in L.A. and so much of the crowd of people who didn’t know who I was until now were singing the song. That was like, “OK, this feels different. Something about this is unique in its own thing.”

How are you processing it in relation to the album?

It’s a really singular, special song. I’d be devastated if I heard another artist put it out. If I heard that song and someone else put it out, I’d be like, “Whoa, no, that sounds like an Ashe song.” I’m really proud of its DNA. But it’s funny because while I have this true pride in it, I also have this distance from it now that it’s in the world and it’s becoming a part of people’s stories. It may mean more to someone who just left someone at the altar than it will ever mean to me. That’s bizarre and cool and awesome. This is the first time in my career that I have a healthy separation from the music. Not in a way that I don’t obsessively love it, but in a way that people’s reception of it is not a reflection on me and who I am and my worth as a person. I’ve never had that until now.

What do you think made the difference in finding yourself getting to that place?

Well, Nicole, I had a bit of a nervous breakdown in 2023, and I almost quit music, and it really took a lot of therapy and gardening and rediscovering why I really loved music and rediscovering that this is what I’m supposed to do. I am uniquely made to be a music artist. I’m uniquely made to be a songwriter. I feel uniquely equipped to handle this world, and I had to relearn that. I had to gain that confidence because I really lost the plot there for a second. Then put out my third record, Wilson, and then Finneas and I made The Dream. We made a whole ass band and put out a record. There was just so much healing and confidence that came from all of that, that now I’m a really solid version of myself.

I have so much to learn. Every day, there’s some new statistic with “Stop the Wedding!” My text thread with the label is like: “This new crazy thing just happened.” so I’m learning on the fly. This is a level of success that I have not had before, but I really know who I am, and I really like her. I love her. God forbid a girl like herself.

Do you think when you were starting out that you would’ve been equipped to handle the level of success you’re having now?

I do feel equipped to handle it now in a way that I definitely was not before. It’s funny, the universe, God, Oprah, whoever’s really in charge, I think [they] knew that this was a time that I could experience it and not lose myself to it. I don’t think that that would’ve have been the case in the past. It’s funny too, because I’ve been doing this for so long. There was so much I needed to learn and go through. You can see it from my first album to now, consistency has only just now clicked in. I think I really started to settle into my personal style and trusting my voice and what I have to say during The Favors album. That’s all been more recent as in the last three years.

It was right. It was correct that it happened this way. The real difference now is I so deeply love my life just as it is. I was deeply in love with my life before “Stop the Wedding!” came out. For all its extraordinary and very ordinary bits. “Stop the Wedding!” having this moment is not the point, it is the cherry [on top] to have a life that I’ve worked really hard for and to protect.

Dune: Part Three's marketing campaign has been a long and generous one, but Warner Bros. and Legendary Pictures knew an extra push was needed in order to compete with Avengers: Doomsday, as both sci-fi blockbusters will be releasing next to each other at Christmas. In its final trailer, Denis Villeneuve's threequel goes all out.

This isn't the first time a Dune: Part Three trailer has left us with more questions than answers, but the in-depth look at the character dynamics and plot beats that await will make longtime fans of Frank Herbert's works raise their eyebrows.

Messiah, the second installment in the book series, is a novel of long monologues and very tense conversations. Action has a place in it, but it's a more restrained and quieter book for the most part — one that deals with the consequences of Paul's (now a space dictator) originally well-meaning actions.

Of course, the cinematic medium requires a very different language, especially when the main reason why these movies have become blockbuster hits is that Villeneuve has expertly balanced the drama and large-scale action. So, it comes as no surprise that his take on Messiah is looking to bring Herbert's concluding thoughts on Paul Atreides (Timothée Chalamet) to life without sacrificing the grandeur that defined the first two movies.

More shocking to readers, of course, is Zendaya's (Chani) much larger role in this finale versus the book, where she was slightly sidelined with a more passive part. Paul's lover walking away from him at the end of Part Two was a major departure, and one that set her up for bigger things in the third entry. Considering how good Zendaya has been in the role so far, we consider this a win... unless Villeneuve completely bungles her arc in the final stretch.

#718. Steinmeier in China: A major state visit in uncertain times

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is traveling to China on a state visit in a period of political and economic uncertainty. Germany is seeking alternative partners in the region but also wants good ties with Beijing.

Eight years have passed since Frank-Walter Steinmeier's last trip to China. Since then, the relationship between China and Europe has changed significantly. The German president plans to spend several days touring China before concluding his visit in Beijing, where he will meet with China's leaders.

His visit comes just as the Chinese Communist Party's Central Committee is convening for its plenary session, a major annual event that foreign dignitaries usually avoid when timing their visits.

The focus of the president's five-day trip will be "Germany's diverse and complex relations with China, as well as the challenges involved," his office said in a statement. In addition to sites of cultural exchange, the itinerary will also include a visit to a Volkswagen plant in Hefei.

The automotive industry, in particular, illustrates the dilemma facing Germany's China policy. China is one of the most important markets for German automotive and machinery manufacturers, as well as for the chemical industry. At the same time, state-supported overcapacity in China is putting pressure on European manufacturers.

Not only that. Germany and Europe are dependent on China for raw materials and technologies, which means they are increasingly seeking out alternative partnerships.

Steinmeier was once an advocate of the policy of "change through trade" — the idea that other countries could be persuaded to become more democratic with the leverage of global trade — which has few adherents left in Germany today.

Now he must now pursue a tougher European line in Beijing. Caught between partnership and competition, Europe leaders recently managed to reach an agreement: Imports of plug-in hybrid vehicles from China are to be scaled back.

"That was a concrete step, but it can only be the beginning," said Michael Laha, an expert on China at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) in Berlin.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Coinciding with Steinmeier's state visit to China, Chancellor Friedrich Merz is traveling to the Indo-Pacific with business representatives. His visit to Japan, Singapore and South Korea will focus on competitiveness, technological upheavals, defense cooperation and critical raw materials. Merz is visiting companies and attending important regional economic conferences in Tokyo and Seoul.

The dual trips are Berlin's attempt to send a twofold message: While the chancellor is "deliberately strengthening Germany's partnerships in the Indo-Pacific at a time of global upheaval," according to Laha, the president is seeking dialogue with Beijing at a time when Germany and Europe are recalibrating their relationship with China.

"This joint trip sends a very well-coordinated message to the Chinese that we remain committed to the partnership but at the same time are taking steps to reduce risk," said Laha, before adding that this is a difficult balancing act that also allows China to save face.

While Merz will be accompanied by a large economic delegation, Steinmeier will be traveling to China with representatives from German culture, politics, and academia. Mikko Huotari, director of the China Institute MERICS, is also expected to be part of the delegation — even though Beijing has imposed sanctions on the institute. "The fact that he is coming along sends a clear message to the Chinese side that we do not approve of the sanctions," said Laha.

In 2021, the EU imposed sanctions against several Chinese party and regional officials, as well as an organization accused of serious human rights violations and oppressing the Uyghur minority. It was the first time such sanctions had been imposed on China since the Tiananmen Square massacre in 1989, and Beijing did not take kindly to them. In response, the Chinese government imposed entry bans and other sanctions against European politicians, scholars, and institutions, including MERICS.

Laha did not expect human rights to play a major role in the German president's trip. Steinmeier is considered a pragmatist when it comes to China policy. As foreign minister, he distanced himself from his predecessor Joschka Fischer, a critic of China, and even criticized Chancellor Angela Merkel when she hosted the Dalai Lama.

On the subject of Ukraine, Steinmeier is likely to be more direct and raise the issue of China's role in the conflict. "Beijing is clearly on Moscow's side," said Laha. In Berlin, however, officials are convinced that China can do more to persuade Russia to engage in serious negotiations and find a solution to the conflict.

Steinmeier may make this clear in his speech at Peking University on Thursday. Germany has "long viewed China's emergence with respect and goodwill," read a statement from the president's office. Today, however, the focus is less on China's continued rise and more on how it uses its growing power.

"If the president points out that Russia used its power to attack a sovereign state, he could be alluding to another regional connection: Taiwan," said Laha. That could be seen as an appeal to Beijing to assume more responsibility for the regional and international order.

To conclude his visit, Steinmeier will meet with China's leadership in Beijing. Talks are planned with President Xi Jinping, whom he has known for nearly two decades, as well as with Premier Li Qiang and the chairman of the National People's Congress, Zhao Leji.

The trip marks the culmination of Steinmeier's focus on Asia during his second term in office. Since then, he has deliberately sought to forge close ties with partners in the region and has advocated for greater diversification. Now China, which is Germany's most important and most challenging partner, will come to its own conclusion.

This article was originally published in German.

HBO has given a Season 2 order to “Youth,” the latest series from Peabody and BAFTA winner Sharon Horgan. The series’ Season 1 is currently streaming on HBO Max.

In the show, Horgan plays a 50-year-old divorcee navigating relationships, her ailing parents and her troubled son, who isn’t quite gelling at his new college.

Horgan plays Alex in the series, which also stars Rupert Friend (Patrick), Sharlene Whyte (Sam), Aran Murphy (Ruari), and Robbie Gee (Frank). Season 1 consisted of eight episodes.
